articles.text: No lost time due to Covid for creative Wildwood dads Piedmont’s traditional and time-honored pumpkin patch has a new home this year. Organized by the Wildwood Dads Club for more than 40 years, the famed pumpkin patch was moved from Coaches Field on Moraga Avenue to the enclosed lunch courtyard in front of Wildwood School. What could be more logical? The patch helps create Halloween spirit while raising funds for the elementary school. Knowing that everything is different this year due to the coronavirus epidemic, Wildwood Dads Club president Brian Learn began coordinating plans with city officials as early as July. “As we [Wildwood Dads] kicked off the year this was one of the first things we focused on,” he said. “We wanted to make sure we knew what we needed to do and how we needed to do it.” The dads will be monitoring social distancing, ensuring that everyone wears a mask, and limiting access to the patch to two small groups at a time. Due to COVID-19 they cannot offer the traditional walk and shop experience, but pumpkin hunters can still point out their favorite gourd to take home. Orders can be place online, and walk-ups are still welcome. The Dads Club followed the Alameda County Safety Protection outline, created a plan and submitted it to the city and county. “It was pretty easy actually.” Learn said. “The fire department came by the first morning and approved what we did.” One thing that won’t be different will be the quality of pumpkins. “I’ve worked really closely with our supplier, specifically because we are going to have a slightly reduced selection. We wanted to make sure we have the top picks of the stock, number ones of each variety,” Learn said. In addition to the traditional orange or white carving pumpkins, the patch has numerous specialty pumpkins. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont has confirmed that it will host a virtual “Pros and Cons” forum for a public discussion of ballot Measure UU on Wednesday, October 14, at 6:00 p.m. The measure is a proposed bond for $19.5 million to rebuild the City’s swimming pool at the existing location. The forum will feature a question and answer period for representatives in favor of and in opposition to the ballot measure and will be broadcast live on The Piedmont LWV YouSpeaking in favor of the measure will be Betsy Andersen, a member of the City Council. Speaking in opposition will be resident Andy Wasserman, whose statement in opposition is in the voter handbook as part of the official ballot arguments. The public is invited to submit questions to be answered during the forum by emailing lwvpiedmont@gmail.com. The forum will begin with each side giving a two minute to opening statement, followed by a question and answer session. Each side will have one minute to answer each question. Each side will then be permitted to present a two-minute closing statement This will be the only ballot measure addressed during this forum. The opponents to Measure TT, increasing the Real Property Transfer Tax on home sales, declined to participate. According to LWV’s rules, both sides must agree to participate for the League to host a public forum. articles.text: The City of Piedmont has aging infrastructure. Our buildings, facilities, streets, and sidewalks need upgrading. City Council and City staff are keenly aware of these needs and are taking steps to address them. In fact, that’s what Measures UU and TT are all about. At a June 29, 2020 Special Meeting, there were two items on the Council Agenda: (1) The Future of the Piedmont Pool and (2) Local Ballot Measures for November. The City Council could not, in good conscience, vote to permanently close the Piedmont Pool without giving voters a chance to decide whether to invest in a replacement. Measure UU is quite simple. Do Piedmonters want to continue to have a public pool for our residents and our schools? Or not? This is not a false choice or an idle threat. Our 56-year-old pool is on its last legs. No matter how well pools are maintained, they do not last forever. The concept behind Measure UU arose from a comprehensive public planning process begun in 2016. The popularity of water sports and exercise has grown enormously since 1964 when the pool was built. The goal of Measure UU is to build a pool facility that meets our community’s needs and can operate cost effectively. Young families and proud grandparents alike want a local pool where all generations can exercise, play, and spend time together. Please join me, the Piedmont City Council, the Piedmont Board of Education, the League of Women Voters of Piedmont, the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, the Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization, and many other community members, and Vote Yes on Measure UU. Let’s come together and build a pool facility we can be proud of for the next 50 years. articles.text: The Right-wing Christian leader Franklin Graham organized a “Prayer March” that was held in Washington D.C. on Saturday, September 26. A mostly white crowd of thousands gathered on the National Mall to pray for national unity, the well-being of President Trump, the Supreme Court, an end to abortion, an end to the pandemic, an end to racism and violence against “people who have suffered unjustly.” Convinced I would be supportive, a friend who had watched the event on Facebook emailed me afterward urging me to find a recording and watch it myself. I know my less than enthusiastic response disappointed him. “You’re against Franklin Graham?” was his deflated reply. How can one be against prayer? How can one be against unity? How can one be against healing? How can one be against Franklin Graham, the flag or a spiritual resurgence in these United States? The answer is Christian Nationalism. A very basic definition of Christian Nationalism is that it is the belief that to be a good American one must be a good (conservative) Christian and that our nation will only thrive when Christianity (the right-wing kind) proliferates and dominates. articles.text: I applaud the Piedmont City Council for its unanimous decision to place Measure UU to rebuild the Piedmont pool on the November ballot. These decisions are never easy, but in this case there are no good alternatives. The pool is in desperate condition and Piedmont deserves better. After a long career in city government, I had the distinct honor and privilege of serving as Piedmont’s City Administrator from 2014 through 2019. During my tenure, I worked with the City Council to address significant deficiencies in Piedmont’s technology systems, civic buildings, and recreational facilities. Most are in need of attention. With limited funds and the benefit of public/private partnerships, the Council was able to vastly improve Hampton Park as well as the main tennis courts. On a relative basis, those projects were “low hanging fruit.” The Recreation Building, City Hall, and the Police and Fire facilities are all in need of attention. Only one facility, however, is in such poor condition that it should be closed permanently. That facility is the Piedmont Pool. Over my five plus years as City Administrator the pool had constant and often significant, costly maintenance issues. The need for the City to subsidize the operational costs grew each year. This could have been rationalized, to a point, as an investment in Piedmont’s youth and resident recreation, except the pool, with its limited size, deteriorating condition, and odd configuration did not meet the needs of the community or Piedmont schools. Over the course of the past four years, the City has made a significant investment to professionally analyze the pool’s condition and work with the community to determine exactly what type of aquatic facility would best serve Piedmont. In 2016, the City Council formed a citizens’ steering committee and held numerous public meetings. The result of this public process was a comprehensive report and conceptual design for a pool facility that fits the site, serves the community, meets the needs of youth for recreation and competitive play, and above all, is both safe and cost effective to operate. Out of deference to the School District’s timing for its bond measure, and subsequent parcel tax measures, the City did not put the Piedmont Pool on the ballot in 2016 or 2018. But a decision about the future of the Piedmont Pool can no longer be delayed. I now live in Astoria, Oregon, population 10,000— similar in size to Piedmont. Residents here overwhelmingly approved a bond measure to build a community pool some years ago. I know from experience that well-designed municipal pools are an amazing resource for a small community. Even though I now live in Oregon, I still want what is best for Piedmont, and I urge you to vote YES on Measure UU. Paul Benoit is the retired City Administrator of the City of Piedmont. “Are you sure we had the software package with us when we closed the Hilton bar?”
articles.title: Necessity, urgency of a new pool in Piedmont

articles.text: Editor: It was my pleasure to get to know Jen Cavanaugh about two years ago when we met during discussions by the Park Commission about how to incorporate the sport of pickleball into the City’s recreation program. Jen attended the meetings of the Commission as an observer for the City Council. She did not play a role in the discussions, but I soon learned of her skill in listening to us players before and after the meetings, seeking our opinions, and providing questions and thoughts for us to consider as we worked with the Commission toward a clear plan for pickleball play. She was a quiet presence, sharing ideas but never intervening in the formal discussions that were taking place. Her engagement was instrumental, in a behind-the-scenes way, in helping the players come to an excellent accord with the Commission that has lasted to this day. Since that period of activism, I have had opportunities to get to know Jen even better. My initial impression that she is a dedicated, thoughtful and intelligent public servant has only been reinforced. Please join me in voting to keep her talent at work for our City. –Lester Ellis
articles.title: Cavenaugh helped city with plan for pickleball

articles.text: Editor: I’m writing to encourage my fellow Piedmont citizens to vote for Hilary Cooper for school board. As a parent of elementary and middle school students in Piedmont, I believe that Hilary would be a great addition to the school board. I worked with Hilary on the campaign to pass Measures G&H, our very important school parcel taxes last year, and I was impressed by her work ethic and her collaborative leadership. Rarely do you see a leader who has both the big picture vision for success, and the desire to work behind the scenes to make sure the details get done. During the G&H campaign, she tracked all of the data diligently to ensure accuracy and kept all milestones on schedule. Hilary was particularly passionate about supporting our teachers via the passage of Measure H. Hilary is committed to supporting all students. She is aware of the importance of differentiation in the classroom, so that each student’s needs are addressed. She listens and she takes feedback graciously. Hilary also has ideas to enhance our district’s efforts with regard to diversity and inclusion. She will ensure all students are heard and feel safe, both physically and socially/ emotionally. We are living in challenging times, and we need leaders who will bring our community together to achieve the best results for our children. Please join me from Chicago where she earned degrees in Economics and Journalism from Northwestern University. These decisions are never easy, but in this case there are no good alternatives. The pool is in desperate condition and Piedmont deserves better. After a long career in city government, I had the distinct honor and privilege of serving as Piedmont’s City Administrator from 2014 through 2019. During my tenure, I worked with the City Council to address significant deficiencies in Piedmont’s technology systems, civic buildings, and recreational facilities. Most are in need of attention. With limited funds and the benefit of public/private partnerships, the Council was able to vastly improve Hampton Park as well as the main tennis courts. On a relative basis, those projects were “low hanging fruit.” The Recreation Building, City Hall, and the Police and Fire facilities are all in need of attention. Only one facility, however, is in such poor condition that it should be closed permanently. That facility is the Piedmont Pool. Over my five plus years as City Administrator the pool had constant and often significant, costly maintenance issues. The need for the City to subsidize the operational costs grew each year. This could have been rationalized, to a point, as an investment in Piedmont’s youth and resident recreation, except the pool, with its limited size, deteriorating condition, and odd configuration did not meet the needs of the community or Piedmont schools. Over the course of the past four years, the City has made a significant investment to professionally analyze the pool’s condition and work with the community to determine exactly what type of aquatic facility would best serve Piedmont. In 2016, the City Council formed a citizens’ steering committee and held numerous public meetings. The result of this public process was a comprehensive report and conceptual design for a pool facility that fits the site, serves the community, meets the needs of youth for recreation and competitive play, and above all, is both safe and cost effective to operate. Out of deference to the School District’s timing for its bond measure, and subsequent parcel tax measures, the City did not put the Piedmont Pool on the ballot in 2016 or 2018. But a decision about the future of the Piedmont Pool can no longer be delayed. I now live in Astoria, Oregon, population 10,000— similar in size to Piedmont. Residents here overwhelmingly approved a bond measure to build a community pool some years ago. I know from experience that well-designed municipal pools are an amazing resource for a small community. Even though I now live in Oregon, I still want what is best for Piedmont, and I urge you to vote YES on Measure UU. articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council upheld a Planning Commission decision to deny an application for a new accessory building and garage proposed at 212 Bonita Avenue. Seamus and Fernanda Meagher, owners of the property, appealed the July 13, 2020 Planning Commission decision to deny the application. Prior to that meeting, the Planning Commission held a public hearing on June 8 to consider an application to demolish an existing narrow one-car garage at the corner of the 14,245-square-foot property and in its place construct a two-story 1,257-squarefoot accessory building with garage. The plan was denied by the commission, and it went to the city council on an appeal. -Project architect Amy Nunes On a new application, the applicants proposed demolishing the existing garage, constructing a new two-story accessory building, and designing the garage so it could provide a turnaround area, up to two parking spaces, create a new trash and recycling enclosure, and install new exterior lighting. These changes were considered on July 13, and again denied The residence at 212 Bonita Avenue, with a garage at the rear of the property. by the commission. An appeal was heard by the city council on September 21 but was denied. The city council may uphold, modify, add to, or overrule the planning commission’s decision. City Attorney Michelle Kenyon noted that council cannot overturn the commission’s decision “simply because it does not agree with the decision. It must make findings regarding why the commission’s decision is faulty.” “The appeal contends that the Planning Commission’s decision is not supported by the weight of evidence of the city code,” City Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell said. Neighbors, Oscar and Betty Rojas, whose house is at the back of the Meagher property, wrote to the Planning Commission expressing their support of the proposed project. “The new structure will provide privacy for both parties. We can currently see into our neighbors’ entire back yard and rear home windows from our upstairs windows, and our neighbors can see into the windows of our upstairs rooms from their main home. The new structure will provide a barrier of privacy that we will both benefit from without blocking any natural light,” they wrote. Real Property Transfer Tax (RPTT) is a one-time tax levied on a property at the time of sale. In the City of Piedmont, the tax is currently at the rate of $13.00 per $1,000 of the value of the property The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee has recommended that minimum additional funding of approximately $850,000/ year for the next five to ten years is needed to maintain the condition of city buildings, parks, streets and sidewalks. Measure TT would generate around $948,462/ year. Funds generated by the proposed tax increase are not restricted and may be used A “YES” vote on Measure TT would be in favor of increasing the real property conveyance tax to the new rate of $17.50 per $1,000. A “NO” vote on Measure TT would be against the increase in the real property conveyance tax and would maintain the current rate of Opponents Say: The proposed increase of the City’s Transfer Tax rate would make it the highest flat rate in the entire State of California and could cost homeowners tens of thousands of dollars when buying or selling their home. articles.text: Authorizes the City to Issue Bonds to Reconstruct the Piedmont Community Pool 2/3 vote needed to pass THE QUESTION Should the City of Piedmont be authorized to issue up to $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to finance the costs of improvements for the Piedmont Community Pool and adjacent areas? THE SITUATION The existing Piedmont Community Pool opened in 1964 and is now in its 56th year. The usual lifespan of most outdoor pools is 50 years. Prior to closure due to COVID-19 shelter-in-place orders, the City was spending approximately $1,000 a day to keep the pool safe and operational. The City believes that residents rely upon the Piedmont Community Pool as a resource to learn to swim, exercise, compete, play, and socialize. It has also been a steady source of employment for local youth. Based on a July, 2020 Concept Study, the estimated cost for replacement of the Piedmont Community Pool including bath house, pools and surrounding site work is $18.8 million. THE PROPOSAL If adopted, Measure UU would authorize the City of Piedmont to issue up to $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to finance the costs of replacing the Piedmont Community Pool and adjacent areas. It is proposed that the three existing pools be replaced with two pools to meet resident needs: a warmer recreation pool with areas for safe water play, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, and physical rehabilitation; and a wider and deeper pool for recreation, physical education, water aerobics, water polo, swim team, and lap swimming. The new pool facilities, restrooms, and related areas would conserve energy and water, comply with state and federal disability and safety standards, and provide restroom access for those using the tennis courts. FISCAL EFFECTS: If all of the bonds were issued and sold, the best estimate of the total debt service, including the principal and interest is $37,446,788. A “YES” vote on Measure UU would be in favor of authorizing the City of Piedmont to issue general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed $19,500,000 for the purpose of constructing improvements to the Piedmont Community Pool . A “NO” vote on Measure UU would be against authorizing the City of Piedmont to issue general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed $19,500,000 for the purpose of constructing improvements to the Piedmont Community Pool Supporters Say: The pool needs to be replaced or it will be permanently closed. Measure UU provides necessary funds to construct a safe, sustainable, and affordable facility to serve Piedmont families, students, and seniors for the next 50 years. Passing this bond measure this year means taking advantage of historically low interest rates and avoiding continued escalation of construction costs in the future. Without the pool, Piedmont would be the only school district in Alameda County without a local pool for swim lessons, P.E, and water sports. Opponents Say: Piedmont should not be taking on $20 million of general obligation debt in the midst of fiscal uncertainty resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic. Piedmont has other liabilities including pension liabilities and sewer loans and shouldn’t be adding general obligation debt to its liabilities. Because of the pandemic, the pool will remain closed for the foreseeable future, so we should wait to see if things return to normal before passing this bond measure. Support – Signers of official arguments/ rebuttals: Robert S. McBain - Mayor Sarah Pearson - Past President, Piedmont Board of Education Nancy McHugh - Retired Principal, Beach Elementary School Steven D. Roland - Chair, Piedmont Recreation Commission Betsy Smegal Andersen - Councilmember, City of Piedmont Opposition – Signers of official arguments/ rebuttals: Andy Wasserman - Retired CFO Larry Miller - Certified Financial Planner • • • • • •

articles.text: The Bay Area sky in September after wildfires 100 miles away. On September 9, the Bay Area woke up to a strange phenomenon. The skies were filled with smoke, filtering sunlight to a low-orange glow. Not only did this create a sense of unease, as if we were living on a Martian planet, but it also sparked curiosity over the unique phenomena we were collectively experiencing. While acknowledging the terrible devastation that wildfires are causing across the Pacific Northwest, there is also some interesting science that can be used to discuss what is going on at home. Use the simple demonstration below to show how light filters through our skies, and use it to better understand his historic event. MATERIALS • Flashlight • Colored cellophane: red, blue, and green. Other colors optional. • White paper PROCEDURE 1. Begin by asking some questions: a. What do you think light is? b. Do you think light is moving or staying still? c. What are some sources of light/what are some things that produce light? 2. Shine a flashlight on a piece of white paper. 3. Grab a piece of colored cellophane and predict: a. What do you think will happen if we shine the light through this [red, blue, or green] filter? 4. Place the cellophane over the flashlight and shine it on the paper. Discuss: a. What happened to the light? b. Did it change at all? How so? 5. Repeat this with the other colors. 6. After testing them all, discuss: a. Why do you think the color of the light changes to the color of the filter placed over it? 7. Now, try combining two cellophane colors at a time. Predict what will happen before testing each combination. Then, discuss: a. Why do you think the light changed to [insert color] when we use these two filters together? 8. Now, try combining all of the colors at once. Predict what will happen, then test them together. Make some observations: a. What did you notice? b. How was it different from the previous tests? c. Was this similar or different to your prediction? 9. Discuss some of the following questions with your learners: a. What new ideas do you have about light now? b. Do you think light travels or stays still now that we’ve experimented a bit more with it? c. Do you think sunlight travels through filters in nature? What would be a natural filter of sunlight? d. Is the light from the sun always the same in brightness, color, or direction? What are some of the different ways you’ve seen sunlight? How light changes colors The size of the tiny waves that light travels in determines what color of light we see. If the waves are long and wide (long wavelength), they make yellow, orange, or red light. If the waves are short and thin (short wavelength), they make green, blue, and purple light. If the wavelength ever changes, so does the light that we see! In this case, when the light from a flashlight passes through a colored filter, the waves change from making white light to making colored light… the same color as the filter. This happens because the filter acts like a screen, only allowing the waves of light that match its color to pass through. All of the other wavelengths (and colors) of light are absorbed by the filter and therefore, not allowed to pass. This leaves only the one color of light traveling beyond the filter. Why does light disappear when all colors are used? White light is made up of all colors of light, meaning it contains all wavelengths. When more than one color filter is used, such

articles.text: Committee is already thinking about Walk for Wellness 2021. “There was so much enthusiasm for this year’s event. Even if we can hold a traditional in-person community walk next year, we plan to include the week-long mileage tracking piece,” explained event co-chair Nicki Gilbert. “We hope the combination of a large community gathering and a week-long celebration of physical and mental health will turn Walk for Wellness into a much-loved annual Piedmont tradition.” The Support Committee is grateful to the more than 30 Piedmont families who sponsored Walk for Wellness 2020, and to Bay Design & Build, The Cooper Group, East Bay Pediatrics, Harmless Harvest, Mulberry’s Market, Niantic and Xantrion for their generous corporate sponsorships. To donate to the Wellness Center, click on PiedmontStore. org. Funds are collected throughout the year. Want to help with next year’s Walk for Wellness? E-mail piedmontwalkforwellness@gmail.com. Terri Burge & Natalie Williamson Walk for Wellness 2020, Piedmont School District’s largest fundraiser for its Wellness Center, had more than 400 individuals who walked a combined 1,200 miles and raised more than $37,000 during the week of September 21. It was organized by the Wellness Center Support Committee, a group of parent volunteers, “We’re thrilled with the success of Walk for Wellness,” said event co-chair KeriAnne Hohener. “All aspects of the event – the number of participants, the miles logged, the money raised – exceeded our expectations.” The event was an inclusive, accessible and socially-distanced event open to the entire Piedmont community. Participants received a Walk for Wellness visor and access to seven maps detailing various walks around town. During the week they were able to log mileage from their walks online, share their favorite walks with other participants, and post photos on social media. Dr. Alisa Crovetti, the Clinical Supervisor of the Wellness Center, expressed her gratitude to the Piedmont community for understanding the need for counseling services for middle and high school students, “It is absolutely crucial that we prioritize the mental health of our students, especially during distance learning,” she said. “I’m thrilled with the response to Walk for Wellness and very much appreciate the community’s support of the Wellness Center.” The Wellness Center Support Ethan & Jeremy Block

articles.text: City recommends to avoid trick-or-treating this year The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) declared traditional trick-or-treating to be a “high-risk” activity for COVID-19 transmission, even with precautionary measures such as sanitizing and social distancing. Although trick-or-treating is primarily an outdoor activity, a statement issued by ACPHD Public Information Manager Neetu Balram said that it would be difficult to maintain a safe distance on porches and doorsteps. Instead, the health officer is encouraging community members to focus on decorations, and to limit activities to household members only. ACPHD also encourages virtual costume parties in lieu of in-person socialization. “Trick-or-treating is a highrisk activity because it increases contact with people outside of your household who may not be as careful about COVID-19 prevention. Parties are high-risk, because mixing among people who don’t live in the same home introduces more opportunities for the virus to pass from one person to another,” Balram said. The department is still encouraging the use of masks, frequent sanitizing, and social distancing. Costume masks are not a substitute for protective cloth masks, but “avoid wearing a costume mask over a protective cloth mask because it can be dangerous if the costume mask makes it hard to breathe,” Balram added. Alameda County residents are reminded that local and state health officer orders are still in effect. Halloween gatherings, celebrations of Dia de los Muertos, and events or parties with non-household members are not permitted unless they are conducted in compliance with local and state health orders. Activities that are not permitted and are considered very high risk are crowded parties, haunted houses, and indoor mazes. Low-risk activities are recommended by the county, to include visiting an outdoor pumpkin patch, carving and decorating pumpkins outside, and preparing traditional family recipes with members of your household. The risk of traditional trickor-treating can be mitigated from high-risk to moderate-risk, if children participate in one-way trickor-treating where individually wrapped goodie bags are lined up for families to pick up and go while continuing to socially distance. The County also recommends that everyone participating should bring hand sanitizer, use it frequently, and wash hands immediately after coming home. The Piedmont Police Department echoed the Alameda County recommendations. “The bottom line is that the city is recommending that people do not engage in high-risk behavior such as trick-or-treating,” Police Chief Jeremy Bowers said.
articles.title: County says trick-or-treating is high-risk for COVID transmission

articles.text: Successor to Jo Hazelett as Council Executive starts Nov. 1 Kate Benson and daughter Kajsa are experienced hikers and campers. The Piedmont Council of the Boy Scouts of America (BSA) announced that Kate Benson has been hired as its new Scout Executive, effective November 1, 2020. She succeeds Jo Hazelett, who is retiring after 22 years of distinguished service in that position. “We’re delighted to welcome Kate to the Piedmont community,” said Seth Hilton, president of the Executive Council. “She brings energy and new ideas that will build on the foundation laid by Jo Hazelett.” “In this succession, we wanted to maintain Jo’s connections throughout our community and across the BSA movement,” said Rob James, Selection Committee chair and past president. “Kate has made those same kinds of connections. We know she will communicate the spirit of our mission for a new era.” Kate comes to Piedmont Scouting from the Silicon Valley Monterey Bay Council, where she is Development Director overseeing large special events and annual fundraising activities. She has 17 years of experience as a Scouting professional, including work as a District Director and Senior District Executive in Portland and Spokane, responsible for fund development, endowment gifts, marketing, membership, and large district administration. Kate and her husband, Neil, have two daughters, Cub Scout Anna (8) and Scout BSA member Kajsa (11). Kate is currently Cubmaster of Pack 785 in Gilroy, is a member of the Order of the Arrow, and was a staff member at the 2017 National Jamboree at the Summit Bechtel Reserve. Kate is a past president of the Vancouver, Washington Rotary Club and an avid rower and musician. “I am excited to be joining the Piedmont Council – clearly an organization that invests in the development of young people,” she said. “My passion is communicating the value and values of Scouting to new audiences, including folks who might not have been associated with Scouts before. Our volunteers spend countless hours working with youth to develop character, fitness, citizenship, and leadership; and through that program, they provide service to the larger community. “Our programs are more inclusive than ever before and I want all families to know they are welcome. I look forward to participating, virtually and soon in person. Piedmont Scouting serves approximately 1,100 young men and women in its programs, ranging from Cub Scouts in grades 1-5; Scouts BSA (formerly Boy Scouts) in grades 6-12; coed Venturing (including the Piedmont Community Service Crew), Police Exploring and Sea Scouts for youth up to age 21, and through Learning for Life, the Piedmont Language School. Over 220 volunteer leaders undergo rigorous Youth Protection Training to policies that are a current model for other youth organizations. articles.text: Kids try on some scary teeth at Piedmont Scouts’ Twilight camp a few days before Halloween. The Piedmont Scout Council is moving forward with Twilight Camp this year, but like many other events, they are conducting festivities over Zoom. It will take place Tuesday through Thursday night, October 27-29. pages.text: 8 Wednesday, October 7, 2020 Kate Benson and daughter Kajsa are experienced hikers and campers. The Piedmont Council of the Boy Scouts of America (BSA) announced that Kate Benson has been hired as its new Scout Executive, effective November 1, 2020. She succeeds Jo Hazelett, who is retiring after 22 years of distinguished service in that position. “We’re delighted to welcome Kate to the Piedmont community,” said Seth Hilton, president of the Executive Council. “She brings energy and new ideas that will build on the foundation laid by Jo Hazelett.” “In this succession, we wanted to maintain Jo’s connections throughout our community and across the BSA movement,” said Rob James, Selection Committee chair and past president. “Kate has made those same kinds of connections. We know she will communicate the spirit of our mission for a new era.” Kate comes to Piedmont Scouting from the Silicon Valley Monterey Bay Council, where she is Development Director overseeing large special events and annual fundraising activities. She has 17 years of experience as a Scouting professional, including work as a District Director and Senior District Executive in Portland and Spokane, responsible for fund development, endowment gifts, marketing, membership, and large district administration. Kate and her husband, Neil, have two daughters, Cub Scout Anna (8) and Scout BSA member Kajsa (11). Kate is currently Cubmaster of Pack 785 in Gilroy, is a member of the Order of the Arrow, and was a staff member at the 2017 National Jamboree at the Piedmont Scouting welcomes Kate Benson Successor to Jo Hazelett as Council Executive starts Nov. 1 Summit Bechtel Reserve. Kate is a past president of the Vancouver, Washington Rotary Club and an avid rower and musician. “I am excited to be joining the Piedmont Council – clearly an organization that invests in the development of young people,” she said. “My passion is communicating the value and values of Scouting to new audiences, including folks who might not have been associated with Scouts before. Our volunteers spend countless hours working with youth to develop character, fitness, citizenship, and leadership; and through that program, they provide service to the larger community. “Our programs are more inclusive than ever before and I want all families to know they are welcome. I look forward to participating, virtually and soon in person. Piedmont Scouting serves approximately 1,100 young men and women in its programs, ranging from Cub Scouts in grades 1-5; Scouts BSA (formerly Boy Scouts) in grades 6-12; coed Venturing (including the Piedmont Community Service Crew), Police Exploring and Sea Scouts for youth up to age 21, and through Learning for Life, the Piedmont Language School. Over 220 volunteer leaders undergo rigorous Youth Protection Training to policies that are a current model for other youth organizations. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. articles.text: the best interests of the city and our residents, which may or may not be in agreement with my colleagues. It is not possible to always reach consensus in our decisions, but that’s how our representative government works -- for the people. 2 – My top priority is to balance fiscal responsibility with a commitment to improving Piedmont’s aging infrastructure and enhancing public services. If Measure UU passes, in two years we will have finished the design process and hopefully be into the construction phase for a new community pool for Piedmont. However, if Measure UU fails, if more than one third of voters decide that they do not want to have a community pool, then our old pool will likely have been closed, drained, and secured, and the city will have to begin a process to determine what to do with the space. Second, this current crisis has made it abundantly clear that wildfire prevention, disaster preparedness, community health and public safety must be priorities. Next, the city is embarking on a process to reevaluate our plans for providing housing of all types and income levels, specifically to meet our state-mandated Regional Housing Number Allocation in 2021. The current expectation is that our allocation could be as high as 600 units. We will look to creatively provide housing that integrates into our community while maintaining the essence of what makes Piedmont special. Lastly, climate change is one of the biggest threats to our health and the environment. The implementation of the city’s Climate Action Plan is a high priority for the city, and we will continue to work with residents to ensure the plan is actionable and reasonable. CONNIE HERRICK 1 – Disagreeing can be productive. Opportunities to air concerns and share ideas lead to cooperation, compromise and the best decisions. We can disagree passionately and argue civilly at the same time. However, if we disagree and argue with the primary intention of “winning” or “being right,” then we shift to a negative space. Tempers flare and feelings are hurt with possible lasting damage to relationships. The Hawaiian word “laulima” means “many hands working together, and is a core principle within the Hawaiian Aloha culture. One set of hands can accomplish much. But many hands can accomplish infinitely more and tackle complex problems. When we embrace this concept, then disagreements become opportunities to listen, receive education and forge new ideas together. I always respect my colleagues and look forward to our “laulima.” 2 – My short list is •. Focus on current priority projects, keep them moving forward to completion and work tirelessly for our City. • Complete Piedmont City Council onboarding requirements. Understand all Council rules of conduct. Attend the League of California Cities New Mayor and Council Members Academy. Complete required California public service ethics laws and principles coursework. • Meet with every City department, Piedmont organization (including student organizations) and the PUSD Board of Education to discuss their priorities and find out where I can support their efforts. Meet as many Oakland, Berkeley, Emeryville City Councilmembers and Alameda County officials as possible to find shared opportunities and forge relationships. • Create a private Piedmont Resident Online Forum on my website for all residents to post their concerns and comments on City issues. Add survey software to my website so I can construct simple, straightforward questions and residents can quickly and anonymously share their opinions. CONNA MCCARTHY 1 – Anyone who seeks a leadership position as an elected decision-maker should understand that robust discussions and disagreements are common. People who avoid conflict may miss opportunities to engage in productive problem-solving because disagreements often lead to positive outcomes. Nevertheless, while I believe colleagues should, when appropriate, challenge each other, it is important to verbalize disagreements without being personal. The world changed in 2016 revealing a deepening lack of civility. Trusted institutions no longer function in predictable ways. Conspiracy theories abound. Name calling is commonplace. Good leaders understand the importance of setting limits, practicing emotional control and establishing expectations. If I earn a seat on Piedmont City Council, I will begin my tenure by listening, observing and looking for opportunities to contribute. I have tremendous respect for currently serving members of council. I will work to nurture dynamic relationships with each of them as we work together for a better Piedmont. 2 – Public safety is a priority. Piedmont residents should go to sleep at night with the security of knowing police and fire professionals will show up with all necessary equipment to provide essential services for a personal crisis, as well as, during and after a public disaster. Our Police Department is housed in a 70-year-old facility. Inadequacies in our existing police facility prevent Piedmont from meeting the national effort to update the 911 system. Our Fire Department is housed in City Hall, originally constructed 110 years ago. Our existing fire facility is inadequate in size to accommodate current fire apparatus and equipment. It is imperative that we evaluate the state of Piedmont’s essential services buildings to bring them to current codes and standards. We must engage the community to gauge interest, support and understanding of the financial implications. Piedmont’s climate action plan serves as a framework for all infrastructure planning. NANCY “SUNNY” BOSTROM No response received.

articles.text: In advance of the November 3 municipal election, Piedmont City Council candidates were asked two questions: 1) How would you approach a situation where a colleague disagrees with you? 2) What is your short list for the first two years that you hope to accomplish? The Post will ask each candidate two questions every week. Responses are listed below. JEN CAVENAUGH, Incumbent 1 – The best councils and boards are made up of individuals representing the diverse perspectives of the community. We serve the public in public, on camera with a microphone for the public to see and hear our deliberations. We share the facts we have considered, the concerns we have, the issues we prioritize, and the variables we weighed. The Brown Act precludes a quorum of council members from discussing city business in advance, so it is highly likely that council members will disagree on certain aspects of a city decision. That disagreement is healthy for our city. In our Council meetings, I seek to understand the viewpoints and rationale of my colleagues when we disagree; and I share mine. After careful consideration, I make my decisions based on what I feel is in

articles.text: of assessment to establish a baseline for each student. I would like to have each student feel that there is an adult on their campus who they can reach out to anytime. I am also committed to an audit of our curriculum around racial justice and equity and to pursuing hiring more BIPOC teachers and administrators when openings occur. These are complex issues, but they are all critical to the success of our students. JASON KELLEY 1 – In our small community, the focus should be on consensus building. This process takes time and a commitment to good-will and respect for everyone’s viewpoints. When colleagues disagree, they must take the time to understand each other’s views by honestly expressing their own and carefully listening to the other’s. They should be seeking a way forward that meets the needs of both while not betraying the core values of either. There may well be times when a compromise cannot be found, and then in our system a vote is taken and all sides agree to abide by the result. This is why it is very important for the school board to be made up of people with a diverse set of interests, backgrounds, experiences, and skill sets. That way, the board represents the whole community and can reach consensus that benefits the most people. 2 – My short list is: • Ensure schools reopen safely and in a way that promotes stability and meets the needs of all stakeholders: students, teachers, families and the wider Piedmont community. Families and educators need as much stability as possible right now, so they are able to plan effectively. • Address the needs of the rapidly increasing population of special education students by adding more teachers and paraeducators. • Engage in planning for how education can best be delivered in the future in light of the lessons we’ve learned during distance learning. There may be place for some form of distance learning going forward for particular students who might benefit from it, including advanced placement students who may want to take classes our schools do not have the population to support. CORY SMEGAL 1 – During my four years on the School Board, there have been times when other Board members and I have disagreed on a decision. What I’ve found to be most important during those discussions is each member’s willingness to listen to other points of view and respectfully discuss differences of opinion. It’s not always easy -- those discussions are in public and can be challenging. My colleagues on the Board are all people that I hold in high esteem. They impress me all the time, not only with their intelligence and thoughtfulness, but also with their commitment to our District. We’ve worked hard over the last several years to develop relationships built on trust and a desire to do what is best for all the stakeholders of the Piedmont schools. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, October 7, 2020 By Allyson Aleksey Part 8 in a series In advance of the November 3 municipal election, Piedmont City Council candidates were asked two questions: 1) How would you approach a situation where a colleague disagrees with you? 2) What is your short list for the first two years that you hope to accomplish? The Post will ask each candidate two questions every week. Responses are listed below. JEN CAVENAUGH, Incumbent 1 – The best councils and boards are made up of individuals representing the diverse perspectives of the community. We serve the public in public, on camera with a microphone for the public to see and hear our deliberations. We share the facts we have considered, the concerns we have, the issues we prioritize, and the variables we weighed. The Brown Act precludes a quorum of council members from discussing city business in advance, so it is highly likely that council members will disagree on certain aspects of a city decision. That disagreement is healthy for our city. In our Council meetings, I seek to understand the viewpoints and rationale of my colleagues when we disagree; and I share mine. After careful consideration, I make my decisions based on what I feel is in Election Preview – City Council candidates Q&A the best interests of the city and our residents, which may or may not be in agreement with my colleagues. It is not possible to always reach consensus in our decisions, but that’s how our representative government works -- for the people. 2 – My top priority is to balance fiscal responsibility with a commitment to improving Piedmont’s aging infrastructure and enhancing public services. If Measure UU passes, in two years we will have finished the design process and hopefully be into the construction phase for a new community pool for Piedmont. However, if Measure UU fails, if more than one third of voters decide that they do not want to have a community pool, then our old pool will likely have been closed, drained, and secured, and the city will have to begin a process to determine what to do with the space. Second, this current crisis has made it abundantly clear that wildfire prevention, disaster preparedness, community health and public safety must be priorities. Next, the city is embarking on a process to reevaluate our plans for providing housing of all types and income levels, specifically to meet our state-mandated Regional Housing Number Allocation in 2021. The current expectation is that our allocation could be as high as 600 units. We will look to creatively provide housing that integrates into our community while maintaining the essence of what makes Piedmont special. Lastly, climate change is one of the biggest threats to our health and the environment. The implementation of the city’s Climate Action Plan is a high priority for the city, and we will continue to work with residents to ensure the plan is actionable and reasonable. CONNIE HERRICK 1 – Disagreeing can be productive. Opportunities to air concerns and share ideas lead to cooperation, compromise and the best decisions. We can disagree passionately and argue civilly at the same time. However, if we disagree and argue with the primary intention of “winning” or “being right,” then we shift to a negative space. Tempers flare and feelings are hurt with possible lasting damage to relationships. The Hawaiian word “laulima” means “many hands working together, and is a core principle within the Hawaiian Aloha culture. One set of hands can accomplish much. But many hands can accomplish infinitely more and tackle complex problems. When we embrace this concept, then disagreements become opportunities to listen, receive education and forge new ideas together. I always respect my colleagues and look forward to our “laulima.” 2 – My short list is •. Focus on current priority projects, keep them moving forward to completion and work tirelessly for our City. • Complete Piedmont City Council onboarding requirements. Understand all Council rules of conduct. Attend the League of California Cities New Mayor and Council Members Academy. Complete required California public service ethics laws and principles coursework. • Meet with every City department, Piedmont organization (including student organizations) and the PUSD Board of Education to discuss their priorities and find out where I can support their efforts. Meet as many Oakland, Berkeley, Emeryville City Councilmembers and Alameda County officials as possible to find shared opportunities and forge relationships. • Create a private Piedmont Resident Online Forum on my website for all residents to post their concerns and comments on City issues. Add survey software to my website so I can construct simple, straightforward questions and residents can quickly and anonymously share their opinions. CONNA MCCARTHY 1 – Anyone who seeks a leadership position as an elected decision-maker should understand that robust discussions and disagreements are common. People who avoid conflict may miss opportunities to engage in productive problem-solving because disagreements often lead to positive outcomes. Nevertheless, while I believe colleagues should, when appropriate, challenge each other, it is important to verbalize disagreements without being personal. The world changed in 2016 revealing a deepening lack of civility. Trusted institutions no longer function in predictable ways. Conspiracy theories abound. Name calling is commonplace. Good leaders understand the importance of setting limits, practicing emotional control and establishing expectations. If I earn a seat on Piedmont City Council, I will begin my tenure by listening, observing and looking for opportunities to contribute. I have tremendous respect for currently serving members of council. I will work to nurture dynamic relationships with each of them as we work together for a better Piedmont. 2 – Public safety is a priority. Piedmont residents should go to sleep at night with the security of knowing police and fire professionals will show up with all necessary equipment to provide essential services for a personal crisis, as well as, during and after a public disaster. Our Police Department is housed in a 70-year-old facility. Inadequacies in our existing police facility prevent Piedmont from meeting the national effort to update the 911 system. Our Fire Department is housed in City Hall, originally constructed 110 years ago. Our existing fire facility is inadequate in size to accommodate current fire apparatus and equipment. It is imperative that we evaluate the state of Piedmont’s essential services buildings to bring them to current codes and standards. We must engage the community to gauge interest, support and understanding of the financial implications. Piedmont’s climate action plan serves as a framework for all infrastructure planning. articles.text: It is long past time for Piedmont to rebuild our one and only community pool. Current residents of Piedmont have benefitted from the generosity of prior residents who built, paid for, and in many cases donated our buildings, parks, playfields and of course, the pool. Their generosity toward future generations has allowed us, as taxpayers, to focus our collective resources on our excellent public schools. It is now our turn to step up to rebuild our failing infrastructure. The two measures on the ballot in November are about repairing and replacing what is broken. Measure UU will allow Piedmont to issue, for the first time ever, municipal bonds to rebuild the failing 56-year-old Piedmont Pool. Municipal bonds are like a 30-year fixed-rate community mortgage, repaid through property tax assessments. Measure TT will align the real property transfer tax – only paid when a home is bought or sold – to match those of Berkeley and Oakland, and use the funds to repair and maintain our city facilities and failing roads and sidewalks. To us, six former Piedmont Mayors, the focus on long-term planning is a sign of pragmatic and strategic thinking. The current City Council unanimously placed Measures UU and TT on the ballot because our failing infrastructure can’t wait. Spending more to repair a crumbling pool facility makes no fiscal sense. Borrowing money at low interest rates to rebuild a necessary civic asset is the prudent decision. Soon the City Council will be forced to make the decision that no one wants to make: to permanently close the Piedmont Pool. If Measure UU does not pass, Piedmont will then fail to provide a basic public amenity that every other city in Alameda County provides to its residents. Whether you swim or not, the lack of a municipal pool would be a profound loss for our community and our schools. Please join us in supporting the future of Piedmont and voting yes on Measures UU and TT. Former Piedmont Mayors: Dean Barbieri Michael Bruck John Chiang Abe Friedman Susan Hill Valerie Matzger
articles.title: Former Mayors make the case for community pool

articles.text: Editor: I am very happy to write in support of UU so that we can finally get a new aquatic center in Piedmont. As some may remember, I was involved in the last major effort to build a new pool (2000- 02. Predictably, the same tired opposition points are emerging this time – parking, traffic, noise, cost, “outsiders,” “now is not the time,” and (horrors!) the specter of swim meets. If we can finally build an aquatic center befitting Piedmont, every member of the community will benefit, from little babies learning to swim; to young children playing to their hearts’ content; to club team members; to high school athletes; to adult lap swimmers; to the disabled; to seniors looking for safe exercise. The aquatic center will also be a gathering place for community members to enjoy each other’s company in a casual atmosphere by the pool. If we don’t build a new aquatic center, Piedmont will be relegated to the ranks of those few California communities that have neither a community pool nor a high school pool, and this will affect the appeal of Piedmont as a place to live, not to mention the effect on property values. So, let’s finally get this done. A new aquatic center will be a highlight among everything that makes Piedmont such a great place to live! Please vote yes on UU! –Josh Bernstein, DDS

articles.text: City’s answers to Frequently Asked Questions about Pool bond. 1. The City proposes to issue $19.5 Million in bonds. What is the actual expected borrowing interest rate assuming the bond passes this year? Municipal bonds can be issued in stages as the funds are needed, and the applicable interest rate is determined at the time the bonds are issued. As a frame of reference, the interest rate as of September 16, 2020 is 2.8%. 2. What is the City’s current total outstanding general obligation debt? The City currently has no outstanding general obligation debt. 3. What is the term of the bond repayment? Measure UU provides that the term of the bond repayment is 30 years with a fixed interest rate. 4. How long will the tax be imposed on properties, and will the amount of the tax ever decrease? Measure UU, if adopted, would impose a tax on properties for 30 years. In the event our property tax roll increases at 3.5% per year (10- year average is ~4.5%), the tax rate per $1,000 of assessed value will drop from $0.26 (if all bonds are issued) to approximately $0.10 in thirty years. The total tax assessed would still be the same but redistributed based on the individual property assessment. 5. How can a property owner ascertain the assessed value of property? Each year, the Alameda County Assessor’s Office notifies all property owners of the property’s annual assessed value. This number can also be found on a property owner’s property tax bill. Residents can ascertain the assessed value of their home on the Alameda County Assessor’s website. 6. How does Measure UU impact the City’s General Fund? Measure UU does not have an impact on the City’s General Fund. 7. What is the proposed concept for replacing the existing pool? In the event Measure UU is adopted, the exact design of the pool facility will be finalized through a public process. The current proposed concept to replace the existing pool is the establishment of two pools: (1) a warmer, shallower recreation pool with areas for safe water play, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, and physical rehabilitation, and (2) a wider and deeper pool for recreation, physical education, water aerobics, water polo, swim team, and lap swimming. Each pool would be larger than the current “medium” and “big” pools. 8. What are the estimated costs of the project compared to bond revenues and what steps will the City take to limit project costs to available bond revenues? The measure would authorize the City to issue bonds with a principal value that does not exceed $19.5 million. In the event the City receives an AA+ bond rating, it is conceivable the bonds would be sold at a premium and Measure UU would provide revenues in excess of the face value of the bonds. The City determined that the $19.5 million figure was appropriate based on rough “hard cost” estimates as follows: $8 million for the two pools to replace the current “medium” and “big” pools, $3.5 million for site preparation, and $6 million for a building to house the pool equipment, restrooms, offices, and community space. If necessary, the concept can be value-engineered during final design development to meet the budget parameters. 9. Can the City repair the existing pool? The City has determined that repairing the existing pool is not a feasible option. The City has been continuously repairing the existing pool since it took over operations in 2011. The repairs required to keep the facility safe and operational have become increasingly expensive every year, and the facility is now at the point where pool decks need to be removed in order to address structural issues. A renovation of the existing facility would require not only major structural repair and equipment replacement but would also trigger significant site work required to meet current health, safety, and accessibility regulations. 10. What oversight is in place to ensure that the bond funds are used properly? Measure UU provides that a bond oversight committee be appointed to make sure the bonds are issued and spent in accordance with the terms of Measure UU. As with any project, staff and the City Council will also work to ensure proper use of public funds. The project will also be subject to the City’s project risk management policy. For more information see the website: www. communitypoolforpiedmont.com.

As with any project, staff and the City Council will also work to ensure proper use of public funds. The project will also be subject to the City’s project risk management policy. For more information see the website: www. communitypoolforpiedmont.com. READ IT IN THE POST Former Mayors make the case for community pool It is long past time for Piedmont to rebuild our one and only community pool. Current residents of Piedmont have benefitted from the generosity of prior residents who built, paid for, and in many cases donated our buildings, parks, playfields and of course, the pool. Their generosity toward future generations has allowed us, as taxpayers, to focus our collective resources on our excellent public schools. It is now our turn to step up to rebuild our failing infrastructure. The two measures on the ballot in November are about repairing and replacing what is broken. Measure UU will allow Piedmont to issue, for the first time ever, municipal bonds to rebuild the failing 56-year-old Piedmont Pool. Municipal bonds are like a 30-year fixed-rate community mortgage, repaid through property tax assessments. Measure TT will align the real property transfer tax – only paid when a home is bought or sold – to match those of Berkeley and Oakland, and use the funds to repair and maintain our city facilities and failing roads and sidewalks. To us, six former Piedmont Mayors, the focus on long-term planning is a sign of pragmatic and strategic thinking. The current City Council unanimously placed Measures UU and TT on the ballot because our failing infrastructure can’t wait. Spending more to repair a crumbling pool facility makes no fiscal sense. Borrowing money at low interest rates to rebuild a necessary civic asset is the prudent decision. Soon the City Council will be forced to make the decision that no one wants to make: to permanently close the Piedmont Pool. If Measure UU does not pass, Piedmont will then fail to provide a basic public amenity that every other city in Alameda County provides to its residents. Whether you swim or not, the lack of a municipal pool would be a profound loss for our community and our schools. Please join us in supporting the future of Piedmont and voting yes on Measures UU and TT. Former Piedmont Mayors: Dean Barbieri Michael Bruck John Chiang Abe Friedman Susan Hill Valerie Matzger After 20 years, let’s get the job done Editor: I am very happy to write in support of UU so that we can finally get a new aquatic center in Piedmont. As some may remember, I was involved in the last major effort to build a new pool (2000- 02. Predictably, the same tired opposition points are emerging this time – parking, traffic, noise, cost, “outsiders,” “now is not the time,” and (horrors!) the specter of swim meets. If we can finally build an aquatic center befitting Piedmont, every member of the community will benefit, from little babies learning to swim; to young children playing to their hearts’ content; to club team members; to high school athletes; to adult lap swimmers; to the disabled; to seniors looking for safe exercise. The aquatic center will also be a gathering place for community members to enjoy each other’s company in a casual atmosphere by the pool. If we don’t build a new aquatic center, Piedmont will be relegated to the ranks of those few California communities that have neither a community pool nor a high school pool, and this will affect the appeal of Piedmont as a place to live, not to mention the effect on property values. So, let’s finally get this done. A new aquatic center will be a highlight among everything that makes Piedmont such a great place to live! Please vote yes on UU! –Josh Bernstein, DDS Family memories made at Piedmont pool Editor: Our family has such happy associations with the Piedmont Pool. We moved here 20 years ago when our oldest child was a toddler. We felt so fortunate to walk up the hill from our house to the pool. There we made friends with other families who had young children, splashing and playing together in the water. As our family grew, our children all took swim lessons and the Piedmont Pool became our favorite place to host summer birthday parties. Now is a good time. Of note, its expansion has been without active recruiting. Even with 30 members, its large coaching staff says there’s plenty of room. The teams has 18 returning riders and 12 who are new. Team members will start recruiting this month. “We are open to expanding. We have 13 volunteer coaches and we feel that we can safely break up into pods. We have a relatively low COVID risk for a sport due to being non-contact and outdoors. We have a natural six-foot separation when riding on bikes. We’re outside in nature and we’re moving, creating a lot of wind flow,”said Aldridge Current plans are to have recruiting rides every Sunday at 10 a.m. until November 22, with the specific hopes of adding more girls to the team. It is an inclusive “no-cut” team, so everyone gets to ride. In addition to individual races there is team scoring, having plenty of boys and girls will help the team with competeive scoring. Piedmont is in the heart of some spectacular mountain bike courses, so it puts the team memebrs into some of the best trails in Joaquin Miller, Redwood Regional, and Anthony Chabot Regiona Parks. Their season is expected to start on December 1 with three practices per week; two outdoor and one indoor dependent on weather. The team is still waiting on official word from the governing body of the National Interscholastic Cycling Association regarding schedules and competitin, but time trials similar using Piedmont senior Nate Willson takes a turn. The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team will be recruiting new members from October 18 to November 22.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Oakland Roots The Roots now prepare for their USL campaign in the fall of next year. The Oakland Roots soccer team suffered a 2-1 loss to Detroit City FC in the NISA Finals on October 2 ot end their season. It was a familiar feeling for the Roots after losing by the same score against the same team in the group stage of the tournament. Prior to the game, the Roots announced that the championship round would be their last appearance in NISA. Next year they will be playing in the United Soccer League, with an opening scheduled for fall of 2021. The game was played at Keyworth Stadium on the outskirts of Detroit. Oakland entered a bit shorthanded at the back without captain Nana Attakora and starting rightback Robert Hines, both out with leg injuries. The Roots have done well up to that point out of the back with David Abidor as their defensive leader at centerback, Daniel Navarro filling in for Attakora, while manager Jordan Ferrell rotated backup Niall Irwin and usual winger Diego Casillas at rightback. The Roots held a 1-0 advantage at halftime, with a goal in the 27th minute by Johnny Rodriguez who scored on a leaping header off a corner kick from Nelson Blanco – both recently acquired players. The Roots had another goal called off after veteran forward Matt Fondy was a couple of feet offside on the far-post. But, similar to their earlier loss to Detroit in the group stages, Oakland’ failure to capitalize on its scoring chances in the first half came back to haunt them. Detroit tied it at 1-1 on a goal in the 65th minute after its super sub, Shawn-Claud Lawson, entered three minutes earlier. Lawson has been Detroit’s sub in each game, scoring in the first 25 minutes. After a failed clearance attempt by Casillas, the ball went to Lawson’s feet like a magnet and he score with a shot to the bottom right corner of the net. The Roots had another chance moments later in the 69th after Blanco sent a nice ball over the top to Fondy, but he didn’t make solid contact on his first-touch Photo courtesy of SFGate The Oakland Roots soccer team lost in the NISA Finals 2-1 to Detroit City FC. shot attempt. The game-winner came in the 84th minute after Detroit sent a long ball down toward the Roots’ penalty area. Oakland keeper Christian Herrera was caught out of position after attempting to approach the ball, then backtracking toward net. The Detroit attacker quickly chipped the ball over Herrera off a volley from the top-left area of the box. The Roots nearly tied the game in stoppage time after gaining a corner opportunity. Striker Jack McInerney found a bouncing ball in the area, sending a shot toward the net. After a ricochet to Fondy in front of the goal line, the ball somehow skipped off Detroit defender Evans Frimpong’s chest sitting on the goal line, skipping it high into the crossbar and out of goal. Abidor had a shot in the 95th minute, but ti was headed off the line by a defender. The final whistle blew moments later and Detroit stormed the field. Good news for local soccer fans. United Soccer League games are scheduled to be shown on ESPN next yeaar.

articles.text: Another week in the NFL season has come and gone, and both the 49ers and Raiders proved me wrong in Week 4. The Niners lost 25-20 to the Eagles and Vegas (Raiders) lost to the Bills, 30-23 loss. KC is allowing 161 rushing yards per game, so it’s possible Raiders RB Josh Jacobs could be on track for his first 100-yard rushing performance of the season. Their use of him will depend on Vegas’ ability to keep the score close. A’s facing elimination The second-seeded A’s lost 5-2 yesterday in the playoffs against division rivals and defending AL champs, the Houston Astros. They dropped their first game 10-5 on Monday. Now down 2-0 in a best of five series, they play again tomorrow at 12:35 p.m. and face elimination in American League Division. It’s been a home runs fest between both teams with a combined six homers in Monday’s game followed by five on Tuesday. The A’s also faced elimination in the best of three AL Wildcard series after falling behind to the White Sox, but survived. For the perennial underdog Athletics, perhaps their backs being against the wall is what sparks its magic. Premier League With the Oakland Roots professiona soccer team concluding its season, we jump over the pond back to England and the Premier League, which just closed its summer transfer window. Teams will not be eligible to adjust their roster again until January. Now entering the International Break for Europe’s Nations League and other national-team matches, play will not resume for the Premier League for two weeks. But, boy, did the fourth of 38 Match Days provide some action. Far and away the biggest shock was Aston Villa – which finished just outside of relegation in 17th – pounce on defending Premier League champions Liverpool 7-2 on Sunday. It was the first time Liverpool FC ever conceded seven goals in a Premier League game and the first time they have allowed seven since facing Tottenham in 1963. Tottenham Hotspur, meanwhile, handed Manchester United a 6-1 defeat last Sunday as well. As things stand right now, Everton and Aston Villa are the only undefeated teams in Premier League. The Toffees of Everton are in first with a 4-0-0 record with Villa already having a third of their wins total from last year in second at 3-0-0. Photos courtesy of NBC Sports Kyle Shanahan’ 49eers were upset 25-20 by the Eagles. They face the Dolphins this weekend and are expected to win. The 49ers, expected to win, were unable to get anything going behind backup quarterback Nick Mullens. He threw an interception which was returned for a touchdown for what proved to eb th winning score. The Eagles only allowed three sacks against SF’s aggressive scheme. San Francisco is now 2-2 and coach Kyle Shanahan is unsure if QB Jimmy Garoppolo, with a high ankle sprain, will be ready for Week 5 against the Miami Dolphins this Sunday. Regardless, the 49ers should be favored, as they were last week. To win, the 49ers’ defense will have to continue playing well against a Dolphins’ offense that ranks in the bottom half of the league. Miami, meanwhile, has one of the worst defenses in the league. All in all, Niner fans should expect a win – or did we say that last week? Raiders The Raiders pushed to within a touchdown, 30-23, but the offense did itself no favors by losing a fumble with the game at 23-16 in the fourth quarter. It led to the Bills scoring their final touchdown. Vegas faces another tall task this week against the defending Super Bowl champions, Kansas City. If the Raiders want to pull off an upset, they will need to limit Chiefs’ quartrback Patrick Mahomes, a highly unlikely outcome. Photo courtesy of East Bay Times The As are trailing the Houston Astros 2-0 in the best of five game series for the American League Western Division championship.

articles.text: Contra Costa. Mission Peak is among the most frequented trails in the East Bay with its sweeping view of the San Francisco Bay. Its 3.1 mile trail to the summit is now open, though the Ohlone Wilderness Trail remains closed. Del Valle, the largest regional park at 4,395 acres, is now re-open for hikers. Limited camping and boating have also been re-permitted with strict capacity restrictions. “Park Rangers and other staff have worked diligently to develop a plan to safely reopen Del Valle in accordance with state and local COVID-19 heath orders,” said park general manager Robert Doyle. “The health and safety of visitors and our staff is our top priority. Visitors still need to follow all social distancing guidelines from local health agencies, in particular, they need to bring masks and wear them when around others.” Although boating on Lake Del Staff Photos East Bay Regional Parks District announced that Mission Peak has re-opened. Del Valle Regional Park has reopened with limited day use and boating. Sibley Regional’s backpacking campsite has reopened to the public at 50 percent capacity. Chabot Regional Park has also reopened camping. The park overlooks Lake Chabot. Valle is opening, the park is not allowing swimming due to harmful algae, meaning consumption of fish is not recommended. Additionally, picnic areas, barbeques, and group campsites will remain closed at Del Valle in compliance with state and local health orders. Campfires, wood-burning, and charcoal barbeques are still not allowed in the parks. Only, gas or propane-fueled stoves are permitted. East Bay Regional Parks District reopened the campsites for two nearby parks, Sibley Regional in the Oakland Hills, and Chabot Regional, which overlooks Lake Chabot. Campsites will be limited to 50 percent capacity. To make camping reservations and for more information, see: www.ebparks.org/activities/ camping.

articles.text: Open water swimmers Fran Hegeler (left), Susan Blew, Steve Hurwitz, Josh Bernstein, Neil Heller, Dave Zischke, Jake Koslowski, Patrick Kennedy, Jacob Tanz, Florence Joliff, and Levy Gerzberg gather for a photo after swimming two miles from San Francisco to Sausalito on October 6. On Sunday, September 6, Piedmont dentist Dr. Josh Bernstein hosted the pandemic version of his annual Golden Gate Invitational Swim to benefit the UCSF Cardiology Council. In recent years, swimmers were transported by boat to the south tower of the Golden Gate Bridge, then swam one mile to the north tower, where they were picked up and returned by boat. This year, for Covid safety, no swimmers rode in safety boats; each provided his or her own transportation to and from the start and finish. The swim went from beach to beach from Chrissy Field in San Francisco to Presidio Yacht Club in Sausalito, a distance of two nautical miles, accounting for the currents. The mid-morning weather was blistering hot and beautiful this year, making for a spectacular swim for the 11 experienced open water swimmers, including Bernstein and former Piedmonters Dave Zischke, and Patrick Kennedy.
