articles.text: There were few ways to connect safely with others during the pandemic, but Piedmont’s Scouts in Troop 4 kept busy this summer with public service and outdoor activities, all in a COVID-safe manner. Wearing masks and social distancing allowed them to participate in a number of adventures during a time when many activities were not allowed. “COVID-19 made it more difficult to enjoy our regular summer scouting activities, like Camp Marin Sierra,” confirmed Troop 4 Scoutmaster Walter Stokes. “But Troop 4 rose to the occasion and put together a variety of outdoor and public service activities that were COVID-safe. “The feedback from our Scouts is that they greatly enjoyed these in-person activities despite the restrictions. They helped us fulfill our scouting goals of physical fitness, character building, and community service,” he added. Some Scouts rode their bikes from Piedmont to Treasure Island and back. Other Scouts got up early to ride the biking trails in Briones and Redwood Regional Parks. They even created their own bicycle maintenance and repair workshop where each Scout, with a set of tools, learned important repair skills. Not only did Scouts have fun, but they earned merit badges as well. Troop 4 also did some backyard camping this summer. Scouts were able to connect with each other via Zoom and review valuable skills while enjoying the great outdoors. Scouts also enjoyed masked hikes in local regional parks. And some even went sailing. Scouts who went on the traditional 50-Mile backpacking trip maintained a “pod” for three weeks in advance to make sure they were all COVID-free when they embarked on the trip. Several of the Scouts even got tested in advance. Several Troop 4 Scouts managed to complete their Eagle projects over the summer. Newly minted Eagle Scout Tom Robinson led a group in painting a mural on a storage shed at Maya Angelou Academy in Oakland, adding color and beauty to the playground. Troop 4 is now welcoming new members. If your son or daughter is interested in exploring Scouts, contact Sarah King at sarahdmertz@yahoo.com. Troop 4 Scouts Lizzy Rachwald (left), Paul Clifford and Zachary Dupree biking across the Bay Bridge to Treasure Island. Lizzy Rachwald (left), Tom Robinson, Charlie Robinson, Mollie King and Sarah King in front of Tom Robinson’s mural on a shed at a school in Oakland. It was his Eagle scout project. Jonah Dupree (left) and Zachary Dupree help at the bike repair workshop. Assisted by his fellow Scouts, Jack Blodgett built a compost box for Greenleaf Elementary School in Oakland to help their gardening and nutrition program. His brother Kevin Blodgett completed his Eagle project by building a fruit storage box for Piedmont Middle School’s Green Team.

Last week Aurora directors Josh Costello and Dawn Monique Williams will interview actor Michael Asberry, who appeared on Aurora’s stage in Exit Strategy and Satellites. articles.text: Summer choir camps are a balance of intensive instruction and peer interaction. trails, and students even get to try organic cuisine grown from the camp’s garden, made possible by restaurateur Alice Waters, known for her Berkeley restaurant Chez Panisse. “Choir camp is a balance of really intensive music training, a bunch of traditions that we’ve developed over 35 years, and being in a beautiful and natural environment,” explained Founding Artistic Director Robert Geary. Each camp runs for about one week, and includes rigorous music theory and choral instruction, balanced with socialization and downtime. Singers rehearse for four to five hours each day. “When young people get together out of their home and school environment, it’s a real growing experience,” Geary said. Given the current uncertainty surrounding the health safety of group singing, Piedmont Children’s Choir decided to offer camp as a virtual program this past summer. Artistic Director Eric Tuan confessed that the students were disappointed by the news due to their love of spending time at the camp. “When the students learned that they couldn’t go to Walker Creek this year, they cried. Camp is such an integral part of the experience,” Tuan said. But the choir faculty was able to craft an engaging experience through the digital medium, while providing something that was different from the online rehearsals that they had in the Spring semester. Maintaining engagement and ensuring students were out of their chairs were key factors when developing a digital camp. “I think it exemplified what the challenge is. We asked ourselves, ‘What is the core of our program? What keeps our students engaged with music. How do we transfer that to a completely different medium?’” Tuan said. Mornings at camp consisted of campfire songs or activities to start the day, followed by a 30-minute music theory class and rehearsal rotations. One advantage of the digital camp was that each student was given individualized choral instruction. “Which is no mean feat for a group of 46,” Tuan added with a smile. The camp faculty sent students home with “camp kits,” which included an electric candle, friendship bracelet material, arts and crafts and other sleepaway camp essentials. In an effort to keep students creatively engaged. As example, this year’s camp was based on a theme of Harry Potter. Students were part of a Potter-themed “house,” and competed against one another to win a prize at the end of camp. Working cohesively and building peer relations are pillars of the camp program, explained Tuan. Utilizing small group classes and one-on-one vocal training in combination with adapted camp traditions helped make it a smooth transition. For more information on choir camps, visit https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/camps-and-tours. Next week: Performing Department

articles.text: Comedian Andy Samberg B e r k e l e y S y m p h o n y announced the launch of “Reading is Instrumental,” a new weekly musical storytime series for children and adults. The series is hosted by the symphony, in partnership with the Berkeley Public Library. It is co-produced by the symphony and the Berkeley Public Library Foundation. Weekly storytime readings began on Friday, September 25, with multi-awardwinning actress Rita Moreno, who read The Runaway Bunny by Margaret Wise Brown. The series continued last Friday with author and Professor Emerita at University of California, Berkeley Maxine Hong Kingston and husband Earl Kingston. The couple read Baby’s Got the Blues by Carol Diggory Shields, a humorous story about the trials of babyhood that tips its cap to legendary blues artist B.B. King. The event this Friday, October 9, will feature comedian and actor Andy Samberg, best known as a former Saturday Night Live cast member. He will read a new book by his friend Jorma Taccone titled Little Fox and the Wild Imagination. The read will begin at 11 a.m. “Berkeley Symphony is proud to partner with the Berkeley Public Library Foundation on this exciting new project that combines the art of story-telling with live music performance,” Music Director Joseph Young said. “The series encapsulates two of my lifelong passions: bringing music to young people and creating community enrichment through shared stories and experiences. There is no better time for our friends and family to come together virtually and see that arts are alive and well in Berkeley.” Berkeley Public Library Foundation Executive Director Kathy Huff echoed Young’s sentiments. “Music and words together are a magical combination,” she said. “We are incredibly grateful for all who have agreed to help make this fun program happen during these exceptional times. We all need stories and music to keep our spirits up, but our kids and families who are at home need them.” Earlier reads are available on the symphony’s Facebook page: ht t ps://w w w.facebook.com / berkeleypubliclibrary/.

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony Music Director Joseph Young will be joined in a one-on-one conversation with pianist Conrad Tao tomorrow, October 8. He has captivated Berkeley audiences in his earlier performances with the symphony. Young sits down with Tao for a wide-ranging conversation, punctuated by piano performances featuring Tao’s vast catalogue of original works, classic favorites, and modern masterpieces. Tao has appeared worldwide as a pianist and composer, and is a recipient of an Avery Fisher Career Grant, and was named a Gilmore Young Artist, an honor highlighting the most promising American pianists of the new generation. His 2018-2019 season began with the New York Philharmonic’s world premiere of a commissioned work, Everything Must Go. He made his Los Angeles Philharmonic debut performHumboldt State University, and Oregon State. Tao’s evening-length collaboration with choreographer Caleb Teicher, More Forever, will be presented by Celebrity Series of Boston, and will make its West Coast premiere at Segerstrom Hall in Orange County. His ongoing electroacoustic collaboration with improviser and vocalist Charmaine Lee continues with an opening-night performance at the 2019 Resonant Bodies Festival in New York. Young’s interview with Tao is the third episode in the “Joseph Young & Friends” series, hosted by the symphony. The series is composed of free online music gatherings, where Young invites colleagues to share intimate musical experiences. The conversations are held via teleconference application Zoom. articles.text: Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players’ virtual series, Bach Shorts, continues this Sunday, Octobr 11, with cellist Jennifer Kloetzel. A founding member of the San Francisco-based Cypress String Quartet (1996-2016), she has performed at such renowned venues as Lincoln Center, the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, the Lobkowicz Palaces in both Vienna and Prague, as well as prominent colleges and conservatories worldwide. She is a graduate of the Julliard School and is a Fulbright Scholar. She has concertized throughout the United States, Europe, and Asia as a soloist and chamber musician. Kloetzel’s performance this Sunday is at 4 p.m. The event will be live-streamed via YouTube Live. She will perform Bach’s popular First Cello Suite, paired with a world premiere by composer Elena Ruehr called Cricket the Fiddler. Ruehr will be on hand to share how Bach’s First Suite inspired her composition. An after-party with the musicians will be held via teleconferencing application Zoom following the performance. The Bach Shorts series concludes on Sunday, November 8 Cellist Jennifer Kloetzel will perform in the Gold Coast Bach Shorts concerts. with cellist Robert Howard from American Bach Soloists and Philharmonia Baroque Orchestra. He will perform Bach’s Fourth Cello Suite and explore Bach’s universal appeal as he collaborates with cellists from Kenya and Colombia. articles.text: Reprise of 2016 production will be in advance of elections Berkeley Repertory Theatre will produce the Sinclair Lewis novel, It Can’t Happen Here, written in 1935 during the rise of fascism in Europe. It will be staged prior to America’s presidential election on November 3. Lewis’ darkly satirical novel follows the ascent of a demagogue who becomes president of the United States by promising to return the country to greatness. The novel describes the rise of Berzelius “Buzz” Windrip, a president who foments fear and promises drastic economic and social reforms while promoting traditional values. After his election, Windrip takes complete control of the government and imposes totalitarian rule with the help of a ruthless paramilitary force in the manner of European fascists such as Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini. The novel’s plot centers on journalist Doremus Jessup’s opposition to the new regime and his subsequent struggle against it as part of a rebellion. In 2016, Berkeley Rep unveiled a new stage adaption of Lewis’ prescient novel. One week after that production ended, the presidential election in the U.S. roiled the nation. Now, the theatre company reprises that production with the same director, Lisa Peterson, but has readapted it as a radio play in four episodes. This time, the radio adaption will take place before the 2020 election. “We’re delighted to welcome back much of the original cast including David Kelly as the candidate Buzz Windrip, and to have Academy Award nominee David Strahairn join us as the liberal protagonist Doremus Jessup,” Berkeley Rep said in a statement. Berkeley Rep Artistic Director Tony Taccone and Bennett Cohen are both co-adaptors. The cast includes Scott Coopwood as Shad Ledue, Deidrie Henry as Lorinda Pike, William Thomas Hodgson as Dr. Fowler Greenhill, Anna Ishida as Mary Jessup Greenhill, and Sharon Lockwood as Emma Jessup. The production can be heard on Tuesday, October 13 at 5 p.m. on Youtube. A live question and answer session with the creative team behind the project will take place following the broadcast. The audio drama is being offered free to organizations across the country. Berkeley Rep intends for the project to encourage the dialogue and motivate citizens to exercise their civic power and vote. articles.text: Everyone knows about Benjamin Franklin. He would be a fine subject for an opera. Richard Wagner could craft a profound melodrama - perhaps along the lines of Lohengrin. But Gilbert and Sullivan would do Franklin with equal aplomb. Rossini would zero in on Franklin‘s love life. After all, Franklin was the darling of Parisienne society, deluding himself on his fluent French. Can you imagine the soliloquy scene during the electric storm? That would surely test the skills of a stage manager. But we need a quick fade to the insanity scene. Those “mad scenes“ were popular in opera. Why insanity? Because Benjamin Franklin actually invented a musical instrument which caused insanity. Like a kid plunking his finger on water glasses, Franklin invented the glass armonica. It was very popular – for a time. But when insanity put the foremost armonica players into the crazy house, that was the end of the glass armonica. The instrument resurfaced more recently when the glass armonica claimed that its old reputation was a lie. Benjamin Franklin had a minor career as a composer. But that is a story in itself – and for another day. Organists come in two categories: church organists and concert organists. There are many of the first category and very few of the second. Supply and demand has a lot to do with it. Though there were many church organists, there was only one Johann Sebastian Bach. Conversely, just as there were many orchestrators, there was only one Beethoven. I discovered the artistry of an Italian organist on YouTube the other day, and he is awesome. Marco Cadario played locally in the Piedmont Center for the Arts a few years ago, but here he played the Center’s beautiful Marco Cadario a wizard of the organ. Steinway. That was awesome enough. But his organ playing is amazing. It’s worth searching on the internet for Cadario playing Rossini‘s overture to La Gazza Ladra. You will discover the very meaning of greatness. Like most people, organists have two hands and two feet. But the organ has as many as four keyboards, a wooden keyboard manipulated by the feet , and a warren of levers to color the sound. The levers are the spice cabinet of the gourmet. With hands flying in all directions, feet running akimbo, and levers opened and closed to color the sound, an organist needs to be many at one time. The ideal organist might look like the offspring of a stegosaurus and an octopus. Benjamin Franklin seated at the glass armonica.
articles.title: Water glasses and insanity (that’s crazy)

articles.text: Jeng is no stranger to exhibiting her work. Home from college last spring because of the pandemic, she painted a still-life series using toilet paper rolls and take-out containers as part of the Art Walk on June 13 sponsored by the Piedmont Arts Fund. Her paintings sold within the first hour. “There is more to consider now; there are heavy events happening in the world,” Jeng said. “But I feel like art is my happy escape. The toilet-paper rolls and take-out containers were more a funny, comical nod to COVID than the difficult, hard aspects of it.” “Ever since I was kid, I’ve liked drawing,” said Jeng who created and helped lead the Art Jam Club at Piedmont High. “It’s a life-long and fundamental hobby of mine. Because I’ve been doing it for so long, my identity and how my life has gone, is because of art,” said Jeng. Discover local artists at the next Piedmont Arts Fund Art Walk on May 2, 2021. To nominate a visual or performing artist in Piedmont for a future article, please contact Kristen Hatcher at hatcherk10@gmail.com Natalie Jeng is currently enrolled at Chicago Art Institute. When Natalie Jeng finished the final painting of her Advanced Placement Art Class at Piedmont High before she graduated in 2019, she had no idea it would hang in a renowned San Francisco art museum the very next year. In August she was notified that she would be among 762 artists from nine Bay Area counties selected to be included in the deYoung Open. Her painting, “The Pale Man”, will be on display starting this weekend, October 10. Fewer than eight percent of submissions were accepted. Jeng plans to attend the artists’ viewing of the exhibit during the weekend. “It is really exciting and really unexpected,” said Jeng, now a sophomore at Chicago Art Institute. . “I’m so honored and I’m so happy to be part of the show,” she said. Artist Natalie Jeng at work in her home studio.
articles.title: ARTS FEATURE Natalie Jeng in Juried Art show at de Young Museum

articles.text: A scene from Kin Dza Dza. My grandma is Russian. She is one of the greatest people in the world. When I have a problem – any problem – I always leave her apartment with a solution. She also finds a treat for me to give to my mom when I get home. But the one type of advice I do not go to her for is movies. The thing is that my grandma is not bilingual so we usually watch movies from Russia which she enjoys and can understand everything. Right now, I think I know what you’re thinking: it’s not that bad, it’s just American movies but translated to Russian, right? Wrong. This amazing woman will find movies that were made when Russia became the USSR. That means crazy plots, strange scripts, and bizarre costumes. The champion of those kinds of movies is Kin Dza Dza. This movie is about a man who goes to buy bread and sees a homeless man, so he and another man stop to help. The homeless man claims that he is an alien who is shapeshifted to fit in. The three of them are arguing and somehow the two strangers get transported to the alien’s world. If you aren’t confused yet, you will be. The two men are now on a new planet with nothing but a pack of cigarettes, matches and a violin. We find out later it is called Pluke and is desert as far as the eye can see. We learn that the inhabitants are human versions of moles because they live underground. As any rational human, they are very confused as to how they got there, and they try to figure out how to get back to earth. We see a flying apparatus approaching, something that looks like a rusted metal bucket with a propeller on top. I am still so confused as to how the thing didn’t fall apart, much less flying you somewhere. But these are locals and they seem to know what they are doing. communicate through one word, KU. This word may look simple but when you say it with different tones it can have different meanings. The two locals get out of there flying mobile, bend their knees, tap their cheeks twice, and extend their arms to their sides, and quizzically ask, ku? As if asking themselves what the heck they are doing there. After five cringe-worthy minutes of trying to talk to each other, the locals get back in their flying rust bucket and start flying away. In anger one of the stranded men takes out a pack of cigarettes and strikes a match to light it. The rust bucket that was flying quickly comes back and the locals start going crazy because of his matches. We learn that this world is deprived of fire, so it is their most prized possession. After trying, one of the locals adapts to their language which is Russian. Now able to properly communicate, the stranded man tells the locals that they need to get back to earth. The locals explain that they need a special kind of fuel to get them home. After flying around, they get to an outpost, which obviously is underground. And since they are visitors, they must wear bells around their noses for some absurd reason. I couldn’t figure that out for the life of me. Being a foolish person, the visitor traded away some of the matches for food, but the traders now with the matches, high-tailed it out of there. They are down by a couple of matches, so they try to find another outpost but with no success. One of the stranded men asks to use the restroom and he is shown the bathroom. After a suspicious amount of time in the bathroom, the second man looks, only to see that the bathroom is gone. The locals said that he was catapulted out. The second man demands that they search for him. While he was looking for him, the locals got back into their apparatus and flew away, leaving the two Russians stranded once more. Eventually they find each other. And that is it for the first of two episodes. I won’t explain the next episode to save you any further trauma. If I had to pick a movie to describe our current year, 2020, this would be the perfect one. It’s so crazy and confusing that it’s as if the Russians predicted the future. If you are into this kind of stuff and don’t mind subtitles, this movie would be perfect. A scene from Kin Dza Dza.
articles.title: Movie recommendations from Grandma

articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SF MOMA) reopened on Sunday, October 4, after about six months of closure due to the current health crisis. There is still time to catch the “Dawoud Bey: An American Project” exhibition, which will close on October 12. Since the beginning of his career, Bey has used the camera to depict communities and histories that have largely remained underrepresented or even unseen. This full-scale retrospective highlights the artist’s commitment over the course of his four-decade career to portraying the Black subject and African-American history in a manner that is at once direct and poetic, and immediate and symbolic. The exhibition includes his tender and perceptive early portraits of Harlem residents, largescale color Polaroids, and a series of collaborative word and image portraits of high school students, among others. More recent projects have taken a historical turn: The Birmingham Project (2012) commemorates the 1963 bombing of the 16th Street Baptist Church in Birmingham, Alabama, in a series of deeply affective portrait diptychs. Lately, Bey has turned to landscapes: Night Coming TenArtist Dawoud Bey derly, Black (2018) depicts, in deep shades of black and gray, the imagined experience of a fugitive slave moving along the Underground Railroad, marking a formal departure from the artist’s earlier work but considering the same existential questions about race, history, and the possibility of bearing witness through contemporary photography. The exhibition is co-organized with the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York City. For more information, see: https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/dawoud-bey-an-americanproject/. SF MOMA is offering two weeks of free community days and free parking at the museum from now through October 18. Daily attendance will be limited to 25 percent capacity. Social distancing is required, and all visitors age 3 and older must wear masks while in the building. Entry will be through timed tickets. In response to COVID-19, the museum has temporarily paused all group tours. The museum opens at 10 a.m. Friday through Monday and opens at 1 p.m. on Thursdays.
articles.title: Dawoud Bey exhibition at SF MOMA closes Oct. 12

articles.text: Tom Holland and Charlie Hunnam stars in The Lost City of Z. The Lost City of Z is based on the best-selling nonfiction book by David Grann, wherein he recounts the early 20th century expeditions of Major Percy Fawcett to the Amazon in search of a dream he called “Z.” The year is 1905, and, as the film soon reveals, Percy’s first expedition is at the behest of the Royal Geographic Society who wishes him to survey what is a questionable border between Brazil and Bolivia. Percy (Charlie Hunnam) agrees, hoping to redeem his family name (apparently his father was a dissolute rogue) in the hopes of being promoted among the ranks of both the army and society. He and his second in command, Henry Costin (Robert Pattison), carrying surveying gear and only a general idea of their destination, arrive at the Amazon River, hire local guides, procure a raft, and thus begin what will be a two-year trip into a jungle that is startlingly beautiful, oppressively hot and ominously dangerous, its gorgeous lethality ever present. England it is not. They encounter not only a hostile natural environment, but also hostile natives who attack them from the shore with spears and arrows. They also come across, in the dead of night, a most improbable and surreal opera performance, organized by a rubber baron who gives them a raft, supplies and local guides. Meanwhile, Fawcett and Costin persevere, traveling deep into the forest, mapping and diagraming the area. It is when they finally reach the headwaters of the Amazon that Percy comes upon carvings in trees and shards of refined pottery, all indicating that there had once been a sophisticated civilization there, something that was unexpected. It was a discovery that would engulf Fawcett’s imagination for the rest of his life. Having completed their assignment and running low on supplies, they make the arduous journey back down river, eventually arriving in England to a hero’s welcome. The Royal Society asks Fawcett to deliver a summary of his astonishing expedition; however, so rigid is the colonial viewpoint held in the England of 1905, the members insist that Fawcett’s claim of an advanced society deep in the jungle is nonsense, The tribes that inhabit the area were considered as “savages,” a practiced colonial point of view. Percy claims to differ and attempts to argue his findings, much to the Society’s disbelief that there could have been a civilization that predated their own. What makes this film compelling is Fawcett’s obsession with his conviction that what he found (and called the Lost City of “Z,” or “Zed,”) was real. Percy has a lovely family that he must leave behind for years each time he returns to the rain forest in search of what many believed to be a myth. His wife, Nina Fawcett (Sienna Miller), is at first supportive. But as their family grows, she argues that though their children who need them both, she insists on accompanying him on his next trip. But it is out of the question. And so, Nina stays behind, feeling the full weight of a patriarchal society. What receives little exposition in the film is the price that Fawcett is willing to pay in order to search for his dream. His willingness to abandon his family for repeated journeys into this unforgiving environment, seems irrational. And yet he returns and returns again until that moment arrives when he and his now grown son, Jack (Tom Holland), who pleads to go with him on one final expedition, are never seen again. What comes to mind is the unforgettable story of George Mallory as he and a guide trekked up the face of Everest, only to vanish in the mist (recently found, frozen and intact, Mallory’s body pointing upward). This impulse to explore is woven into the tapestry of the human condition, the unknown ever seductive, beckoning, harrowing, and often ultimately demanding a sacrifice that can become irrevocable. In The Lost City of Z it’s the Amazon. But it’s also Everest, the Arctic, the ocean’s horizon, all involving travels both outward and inward, just beyond the reach and just beyond the grasp. The Lost City of Z. Starring Robert Pattison, Charlie Hunnan and Sienna Miller. 140 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS The Lost City of Z a search for an ancient civilization

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré If you have been exploring the extraordinary works from Studio Ghibli, you have discovered that the lead character is often a young female who is simultaneously fragile and fearless. When Marnie Was There is based on the 1967 fantasy book by English author Joan G. Robinson. The protagonist is a lonely, androgynous 12-year-old girl named Anna (Kiernan Shipka) who lives in urban Sapporo, Japan. Because she is asthmatic, her foster mother, Mrs. Kadoya (Kathy Bates), sends her to live with relatives in the country – a windswept, marshy, seaside area that will, hopefully, restore Anna’s health. While exploring the marshes, Anna unexpectedly comes across a deserted mansion that seems eerily familiar. It’s there that she encounters a strange, mysterious girl of her own age, very western looking, with striking blonde hair and wearing outof-date clothes. Unexpectedly, the two develop a friendship and begin to share dreams and diaries which, for Anna, lead to moments of self-discovery and revelation. Gradually she begins to emerge from her reclusive shell, growing more and more captivated with the house and is inhabitant, a spectral girl named Marnie. The story, languid and almost wistful, gently pulls the audience into its inherent magic, while adding goosebump moments, especially when the girls wander through a seemingly haunted lighthouse during a rainstorm. When Marnie Was There is compelling in so many ways: softly sinister at times, enigmatic, and also a coming-of-age tale with tom-boyish Anna beginning to come to terms not only with her past but with her future. The artistry is breathtaking, always hand drawn, possessing a level of exceptional animé that is the Studio Ghibli’s brand. The images – a Monet-like forest, ocean waves cresting across an inlet bay, bucolic scenes with long, contrasting shadows in a dew-covered garden – add to the richness and enchantment of the remarkable fable. When Marnie Was There (2014). Animé from Studio Ghibli. Written and directed by Hiromasa Yonebayashi. With the voices of Hailee Seinfeld, Kiernan Shipka, and Kathy Bates. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated PG.

By Chris Honoré The Lost City of Z is based on the best-selling nonfiction book by David Grann, wherein he recounts the early 20th century expeditions of Major Percy Fawcett to the Amazon in search of a dream he called “Z.” The year is 1905, and, as the film soon reveals, Percy’s first expedition is at the behest of the Royal Geographic Society who wishes him to survey what is a questionable border between Brazil and Bolivia. Percy (Charlie Hunnam) agrees, hoping to redeem his family name (apparently his father was a dissolute rogue) in the hopes of being promoted among the ranks of both the army and society. He and his second in command, Henry Costin (Robert Pattison), carrying surveying gear and only a general idea of their destination, arrive at the Amazon River, hire local guides, procure a raft, and thus begin what will be a two-year trip into a jungle that is startlingly beautiful, oppressively hot and ominously dangerous, its gorgeous lethality ever present. England it is not. They encounter not only a hostile natural environment, but also hostile natives who attack them from the shore with spears and arrows. They also come across, in the dead of night, a most improbable and surreal opera performance, organized by a rubber baron who gives them a raft, supplies and local guides. Meanwhile, Fawcett and Costin persevere, traveling deep into the forest, mapping and diagraming the area. It is when they finally reach the headwaters of the Amazon that Percy comes upon carvings in trees and shards of refined pottery, all indicating that there had once been a sophisticated civilization there, something that was unexpected. It was a discovery that would engulf Fawcett’s imagination for the rest of his life. Having completed their assignment and running low on supplies, they make the arduous journey back down river, eventually arriving in England to a hero’s welcome. The Royal Society asks Fawcett to deliver a summary of his astonishing expedition; however, so rigid is the colonial viewpoint held in the England of 1905, the members insist that Fawcett’s claim of an advanced society deep in the jungle is nonsense, The tribes that inhabit the area were considered as “savages,” a practiced colonial point of view. Percy claims to differ and attempts to argue his findings, much to the Society’s disbelief that there could have been a civilization that predated their own. What makes this film compelling is Fawcett’s obsession with his conviction that what he found (and called the Lost City of “Z,” or “Zed,”) was real. Percy has a lovely family that he must leave behind for years each time he returns to the rain forest in search of what many believed to be a myth. His wife, Nina Fawcett (Sienna Miller), is at first supportive. But as their family grows, she argues that though their children who need them both, she insists on accompanying him on his next trip. But it is out of the question. And so, Nina stays behind, feeling the full weight of a patriarchal society. What receives little exposition in the film is the price that Fawcett is willing to pay in order to search for his dream. His willingness to abandon his family for repeated journeys into this unforgiving environment, seems irrational. And yet he returns and returns again until that moment arrives when he and his now grown son, Jack (Tom Holland), who pleads to go with him on one final expedition, are never seen again. What comes to mind is the unforgettable story of George Mallory as he and a guide trekked up the face of Everest, only to vanish in the mist (recently found, frozen and intact, Mallory’s body pointing upward). This impulse to explore is woven into the tapestry of the human condition, the unknown ever seductive, beckoning, harrowing, and often ultimately demanding a sacrifice that can become irrevocable. In The Lost City of Z it’s the Amazon. But it’s also Everest, the Arctic, the ocean’s horizon, all involving travels both outward and inward, just beyond the reach and just beyond the grasp. The Lost City of Z. Starring Robert Pattison, Charlie Hunnan and Sienna Miller. 140 min. Rated PG-13. A scene from Studio Ghibli’s When Marnie Was There. articles.text: And Bill does this in spades.” Barbara Thompson reflected on her move back to California in 2004, after 11 moves around the country, “and just as many churches.” “We thought we would try Piedmont Community Church first, but after hearing one sermon by Bill, we knew we had found the perfect minister,” she said. Rich Thompson, sharing his wife’s sentiments, added that he stands in awe of McNabb’s ability to conceive, create, and deliver wonderful high-impact messages Sunday after Sunday. “You are leaving us with a strong, vibrant, financially sound church community, and a foundation on which to build for the future,” Thompson said in a final message to McNabb. Though retired, McNabb and his wife Maureen remain busy and still living at home in Piedmont. For church member stories, see: https://www.youtube.com/ w a t c h? v =l JS nV YJQ t OE &- feature=youtu.be. For stories by church staff members, see: ht t p s://w w w.yout u b e.c om / watch?v=e7VephCfx_A&feature=youtu.be. Photos by Michael Barber Retiring Senior Minister Dr. William McNabb delivers a last video message for Piedmont Community Church. Piedmont Community Church members and staff reflected on Dr. William McNabb’s time as Senior Minister in a touching virtual celebration last Sunday, September 27. The church presented a final video tribute to McNabb following his last sermon as he retired after 19 years at the helm. Long-time Church Office Manager Jean Leahy said that she has seen a number of ministers come and go, but added that she has especially enjoyed the past 19 years with McNabb. Associate Minister Rev. Dr. Don Ashburn said that he and McNabb shared a great dynamic in the church. “I think it’s been a great strength of us as a team,” Ashburn said. Leslie Quantz, Director of Children’s Ministries, shared that she had no prior experience with youth ministries when she started with the church, but that McNabb became her mentor. “When he called and asked me to do the job on an interim basis, I was really shocked,” she recalled. “I took the job and asked to become permanent after a few months because I loved it so much. I think a lot of that has to do with Bill’s guidance and support.” Quantz has been with the church for over 13 years. “Life’s way too short to work with people you don’t like. I really appreciate how Bill nurtured the family aspect of our whole staff,” said Rev. Scott Kail, the youth minister. Music Director Dr. Steve Main gathered jazz violinist Mads Tolling, guitarist Mitch Polzak and vocalist Sylvia Sudat for a musical tribute celebrate McNabb’s retirement. Each performance was done separately and edited together in a digital format. The group performed “Livin’ in the Name of Love” by Jim Rushing and Marshall Chapman, with Main, the church organist and choir director, on bass. Reflecting on his first meeting with McNabb at the Claremont Hotel in Berkeley, Main said, “While we were waiting for our table, Bill stopped and talked about the extensive wines of the Bay Area that he loved, and he remarked on the local produce we were about to eat in the meal. What became clear to me was that he was a guy who experiences his spirituality through the full enjoyment and delight of what’s right in front of him,” he said. Church members also offered their well wishes to McNabb. “Bill was probably the reason that we joined Piedmont Community Church. I was so drawn to the sermons. We’ve always appreciated how thoughtful they are, how much perspective they bring to life,” said Gwedolyn Osburn. Her husband, Mike Osburn, was baptized by McNabb along with their three daughters. Bob Coleman, always wry, said, “The trick in preaching is coming up with the right message at the right time in the right way. Rich and Barbara Thompson Jean Leahy Bob Coleman Gwedolyn and Mike Osborn McNabb exits the church after his final sermon on September 27. EAST BAY AGENCY FOR CHILDREN AUXILIARY PRESENTS

articles.text: The other day I stepped outside and felt that “Fall feeling.” Right now, it can be hard to detect here in the Bay Area, given how the smoke keeps settling in. Many of us are experiencing anxiety about our beloved wine country being up in flames and the impact that the fires have on everyone’s lives. Last month in this column I described a recent trip Darshan and I took to tour the studio of our beloved glass-blowing vendors, Bel Vetro in Healdsburg. This month I worry about their wellbeing and the safety of their beautiful space. As of this writing, fires are still burning in Napa County and evacuation orders continue to be in effect. One of our favorite woodworker’s homes is threatened. Bel Vetro’s owners, who have put their hearts and souls into their company, have had to evacuate twice this year. And two of our clients’ homes are in peril. All of that hard work, the love, the time, and the living that’s gone into and gone on in their homes and studios. And the heartache of the iconic Meadowood Resort, now burned. How is this possible? We need to get serious about global warming. Since I’m on this tangent already, may I suggest that you watch Kiss the Ground on Netflix for ideas on how we can heal this planet. Fires, and the heartache of that first Presidential debate last week? Heartburn. So, in light of all of this, may I say that in spite of everything, I am having a really great day. I’m noticing lately how, if somebody is doing well, they are afraid to say they are. I am afraid to say I am because it might sound like I am not concerned about what is going on in politics, institutionalized racism, the fires, COVID, all the things. And frankly, these days, I have a similar feeling when I talk about creating beautiful spaces for people. If not everyone can live in a beautiful, thoughtfully curated home, then it’s not okay for me to be an interior designer. Period. How do I make sense of the Haves and the Have-Nots? This question takes me back to my time studying and meditating with the Center for Spiritual Living. There is a principle I first heard there, and that I am reminding myself of today. “My feeling bad for someone does not do anything to make their situation better.” What do guilt and sadness do for them? Nothing. However, if I feel great, if I am engaged in self-care. if I am resourced, I’m going to want to help other people. In light of the needs of the sick, the issues being fought for in the Black Lives Matter movement, the destruction of homes and businesses in the fires, how do we go on and feel okay about what we are doing as beauty-makers? articles.text: It’s that time of year when, if you work for a medium-to-large employer, you’ve got some decisions to make, because it’s open enrollment time. Depending on your situation you may have been working remotely for a while, but, even so, you will likely have the opportunity to review your benefits package and make changes. You’ll want to make the right moves because your choices can have a big financial impact on your life. Take a close look at these key areas of your benefits program: be enough for your needs. If you only had this group policy, but your family situation has recently changed through marriage or the addition of a new child, you may well need to add some private insurance. • Health insurance Think about your health care needs over the coming year – will you or someone in your family be coping with a chronic illness or facing a surgery? Will you need to at least consider testing and possible treatment for COVID- 19? In any case, make sure you’re choosing the right plan for your needs. And pay close attention to any changes in your health insurance, such as whether the plan’s provider networks have changed – you may want to make sure your own doctor is still in-network. Also, check to see if you can reduce your health care premiums by taking part in a wellness program or health-risk assessment. • Disability insurance In addition to offering group life insurance, your employer may provide short-term disability insurance as an employee benefit. Like group insurance, this disability coverage may not cost you anything, but it may not be adequate – typically, short-term disability only replaces part of your income for three to six months. And while you may never need to miss work for an extended period of time, you never can tell – after all, more than one in four 20-year-olds will become disabled before they retire, according to the U.S. Social Security Administration. You may want to consider purchasing your own long-term disability policy on top of the coverage offered by your employer. • Life insurance Your employer may offer a group life insurance policy for free, or for a small amount. It’s probably worth your while to take this coverage, but it may not • Retirement plan You can probably make changes to your 401(k) or similar employer-sponsored retirement plan at any time, but why not look at it now, when you’re reviewing all your benefits? If you can afford to increase your contributions, you probably should, because a 401(k), with its tax advantages and ease of contribution through paycheck deductions, is a great way to save for retirement. At a minimum, put in enough to earn your employer’s match. You’ll also want to review your 401(k)’s investment mix. Is it still providing you with significant growth potential within the context of your individual risk tolerance? Over time, you may need to make some adjustments, either because an investment is underperforming or because you’re getting close to retirement and you need to reduce your risk exposure. In any case, it’s a good idea to check up on your 401(k)’s investments at least once a year. Your employee benefits are an important part of your overall financial picture – so do what you can to get the most from them. articles.text: One of the unfortunate side effects of the excessive number of cars (and traffic) in our built environment is the overabundance of required parking that goes along with it. Walking through Piedmont, it is clear that one reason it is so nice is the absence of large paved public parking lots so common in other communities. Even in our town center with a church, community center, art center, city hall, market, banks, offices, high school, middle school, and alternative school, there are no large, often desolate parking lots that are so destructive to the desired pedestrian scaled character and fabric a city. We are fortunate that this city was founded and laid out in an era before the ubiquitous auto dominance in our culture. If this city were designed today, conforming to typical current required parking standards, the town center would look nothing like it does. It would look instead like The main town center public parking is wonderfully designed. A curved narrow aisle visually breaks up the lot, cars are screened by planting on two sides, the lot is softened by larger trees, and there is a clear, simple search pattern. Curbside parking is generally a good thing. It is convenient, slows street traffic, and provides a barrier between pedestrians and the traffic flow of the street. Although currently a necessity in our culture, most parking lots are simply not very nice. They take up an incredible amount of space and impermeable paving and make up a large no-man’s land between the users and the facilities they serve. Often, they sit sparsely used or empty on off hours.

It would look instead like The main town center public parking is wonderfully designed. A curved narrow aisle visually breaks up the lot, cars are screened by planting on two sides, the lot is softened by larger trees, and there is a clear, simple search pattern. Curbside parking is generally a good thing. It is convenient, slows street traffic, and provides a barrier between pedestrians and the traffic flow of the street. Although currently a necessity in our culture, most parking lots are simply not very nice. They take up an incredible amount of space and impermeable paving and make up a large no-man’s land between the users and the facilities they serve. Often, they sit sparsely used or empty on off hours. There are numerous nice small parking lots located throughout the central area of the city. many areas of the surrounding newer communities, often essentially parking lots with isolated buildings in them. The interesting thing is that the reasonable small parking lots we have somehow work. Everybody finds parking places for all the activities. How is this possible? Several things come to mind. First, all our parking lots are shared by the surrounding uses. The church for example doesn’t have its own lot separate from the community center nor does the city hall have a separate lot from the art center. Secondly, there is curbside parking everywhere. Newer communities often prohibit this in central areas in what I consider an ill-conceived effort to move traffic faster on the streets. Third, a fair amount of people walk to events – the church, the store, city hall and neighbors’ houses, reducing the traffic and also the need for parking. Residential private parking on individual lots is the other part of the parking equation. The nicest homes, and coincidentally the nicest residential streets, are those that have the car parking clearly subordinate in the architectural design. There are a number of ways this is accomplished. A number of streets in town have associated mid-block alleys that provide auto access to rear facing garages at the back of the lots. We also see many detached front accessed garages placed to the rear of the property, away from and not competing with the street facade. And finally, there are many homes with attached front facing garages that are recessed or cleverly located to the side so they are not dominant in the street-side architecture of the home. Once parked cars and/or garage doors are given equal or more visual importance than the pedestrian entrance of a home, the scale is destroyed and the whole character of the home is compromised. We will discuss more of this in a future column. Next: Entries and Porches Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for close to 30 years. He can be reached at Will@MakingDesignSense.com. articles.text: Oven-roasted Brussels sprouts and delicata squash are a clear signal we’re transitioning from summer to autumn meals. This is my third published recipe using delicata squash in as many years. We enjoy this seasonal favorite countless times throughout fall and winter. Creating dishes using minimal ingredients with maximal taste is the key in these days of home cooking. A spice blend will do the heavy lifting on seasoning this dish. It’s the key behind this five-ingredient recipe. In addition to a chile blend, I’ve prepared versions of roasted vegetables using curry blends, harissa, Ras el Hanout, and Chinese Five Spice. You get to take your pick. This recipe has endless adaptations with vegetables, aromatics, spices and herbs. I happen to have a favorite spicery where I’ve purchased freshly milled herbs, chiles, and spices for years, Local Spicery. It’s important to like the spice blends right out of the jar to minimize fussing and doctoring them to suit your taste buds. The idea is that they make things easy, so go with a brand that works for you. There is no shortage of local spice shops for that personal touch, and there is an abundant variety of spice blends at local markets. Any flavor profile you enjoy will work here. So will a simple dusting of sea salt and freshly ground pepper. Five ingredients deliver an outstanding result. F-I-V-E! • • • • deep green, sliced in half lengthwise 1 pound delicata squash, ends trimmed, halved and seeds removed; sliced into 1/2-inch thick pieces 1 tablespoon olive oil 1 tablespoon chile powder blend, or substitute any preferred spice blend 1/2 teaspoon sea salt, to taste if your spice blend is salt-free INSTRUCTIONS Place an oven rack on the middle rack of the oven and preheat the oven to either 350° F on the “convection-roast” setting, or 400° F on the “bake” setting. Place the sliced Brussels sprouts and delicata squash on a sheet pan and drizzle with 1 tablespoons of olive oil. Stir the Brussels sprouts and squash pieces around to cover each with olive oil. Add more oil if needed. Arrange the slices into a single layer. Place the pan of Brussels sprouts and squash into the oven and roast for about 12 – 15 minutes, when you see some browning on them, remove the pan from the oven. Using a spatula, move the pieces close together and sprinkle with chile powder blend (or other spice blend) and salt to taste. Stir to mix, then spread out into an even layer and return the pan to the oven. Roast an additional 5 – 7 minutes until both the Brussels sprouts and squash are golden-brown. Test the vegetables with a fork to check they are tender but still provide slight resistance. You don’t want them mushy. Chile Roasted Brussels Sprouts and Delicata Squash Makes about four cups INGREDIENTS • 1 pound Brussels sprouts, For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com

articles.text: For the first time in its 22-year history, the annual Piedmont Harvest Festival was held online rather than in Piedmont Park due the current health pandemic. The Recreation Department asked residents to send in photographs of the items they otherwise would have brought to the Community Hall as part of the bounty of samples of home-grown foods. Mayor Bob McBain picked the winners in a random drawing. Rami Albert was the winner of the Edible Food Contest with a picture of cucumbers that were grown locally. The honor came with a $60 gift certificate from Ace Garden Center. Everyone who entered the contest received a participation ribbon and was entered into the random drawing. Piedmont Garden Club sponsored a youth art contest this year as well. Piedmont kids ages 14 and younger were asked to download a coloring poster, create their own vegetable drawing, or make a collage from a nature scavenger hunt page. The winner was 8th grader Sophie Glass, whose art work was chosen by a random draw. Glass received a $30 gift certificate from Village Market for her entry. Harvest Festival founder and former mayor Susan Hill noted that there were more entrants this year than ever before. The festival will return for its 23rd year in 2021. Rami Albert’s home-grown cucumbers won the Harvest Festival Edible Food Contest this year. A pastel by Sophie Glass won the youth art contest at the virtual Piedmont Harvest Festival in September.
articles.title: Harvest Festival announces winners of Edible Food Contest

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: In support of Hilary Cooper for school board I am writing in strong support for Hilary Cooper for the Piedmont School Board. I have a long history of advocacy for S.T.E.A.M. subjects in town including co-founding Piedmont Makers in 2014 and serving as President. I first met Hilary when she was the PMS parent club president and we were starting Makers. Hilary was very supportive of our start-up process including securing part of our “seed” funding from her parent club budget. She saw the value that Makers could bring to Piedmont. Since then it has grown to encompass many programs including School Maker Faires, Makerspaces, over 30 Robotics teams, and our $400,000 fundraising campaign to outfit the engineering lab in the new S.T.E.A.M. building. Based on my experiences with Hilary, I believe she would continue to be a strong supporter of innovation in our district. In order to meet the constantly evolving demands of distance learning, getting our kids back to school safely, and keeping our curriculum and technology up-to-date is important. We cannot think of our pre-COVID curriculum and teaching models as the world changes around us. I worked with Hilary when I was on the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) board of directors and Hilary was co-chair of the Giving Campaign. She deeply understands the role that PEF plays in our school budgeting process which will only get more important moving forward. Most recently she co-chaired the successful Measures G&H campaign, which provides approximately 30% of the district’s operating budget. Her ability to lead strategic campaigns to successful outcomes is proof of the impact she can bring on the school board. Hilary brings over 11 years of experience supporting our schools in various capacities as a volunteer. I know that she would put all of her skills and experience to work making our schools the best they can be for all learners. Please join me in voting for Hilary Cooper for the school board. articles.text: Editor: From the moment I met Veronica Thigpen at a community event, I immediately felt a connection with her. Her warmth, kindness and sincerity resonated with me. I’ve gotten to know Veronica very well, having worked with her closely on several projects. Juggling multiple tasks under the pressure of looming deadlines, she has demonstrated the ability to make quick, yet thoughtful decisions, while remaining calm and positive. Her receptivity to input from all team members created a supportive environment that encouraged the sharing of ideas. After living in Piedmont for over 16 years, it was Veronica, a relative newcomer to Piedmont, who made me feel, for the first time, a part of the Piedmont Community. Veronica’s decision to run for School Board excites me. In addition to the personal qualities she has demonstrated, Veronica has the experience and insight to bring our district into the light of current thought. Through her focus on equity, she will help the Board address the social issues of our time, and help our children gain the tools to face an ever-changing world while maintaining top level academics. Join me in voting. Veronica Thigpen for Piedmont School Board. –Suzanne Lane
articles.title: Veronica Thigpen well-suited to be on school board

articles.text: old enough for school, I would walk to the pool in the middle of the day for a swim. Most days I would see someone I knew, and often we would kick for a while together or chat in the locker room. No matter how I felt going to the pool, I always felt great getting out of the water. Every time I swam in that pool, I felt an overwhelming sense of gratitude, hope and possibility. The Piedmont Pool has been a place where people of all ages have formed many happy memories. But pools do not last forever, and Piedmont’s beloved pool is 56 years old and failing. I have watched as the staff has patiently tried to patch it together time and time again, but its age-related deterioration is irreversible. If we want future generations of Piedmonters to have access to a local swimming pool, we need to get going on a replacement. Please join me and our family in supporting Measure UU, so current and future generations can create their own happy memories right here in the middle of our beautiful town. We are voting Yes on Measure UU and hope you do too. –Sarah Pearson, Evan, Emma, Abigail and Nate Seevak

articles.text: A “Spare the Air” alert was extended for the San Francisco Bay Area, including Piedmont, through tomorrow, Thursday, October 7, the Bay Area Air Quality Management District said yesterday, Tuesday, October 6. The region’s air quality is being negatively impacted by the destructive Glass Fire that continues to burn through Sonoma and Napa counties. “While most of the Bay Area has experienced cleaner air over the past few days, localized and intermittent smoke impacts will continue near the Glass Fire,”said Jack Broadbent of Bay Air Aire Quality District. “Bay Area residents should continue to be vigilant about air quality conditions over the next couple of days. As fire containment efforts progress and more favorable weather conditions move into the region, we expect more widespread relief from smoke starting this weekend.” When Spare the Air warnings are in effect, people are advised to limit their times outdoors, especially those with who are sensitive to air conditions. Additionally, the use of fireplaces, wood stoves, pellet stoves, outdoor fire pits or other wood-burning devices is prohibited. The Glass Fire began early on September 27. Thousands of people have been evacuated in and aroudn Calistoga, 66,840 acres have burned in the North Bay and 1,411 structures have been destroyed. The fire, which has burned through many vineyards and wineries, is 50 percent contained as of yesterday. The weather in the Bay Area is expected to improve from a wildfire risk standpoint throughout the week, and some precipitation is expected this weekend. However, Fire Chief Bret Black said that wildfire season is a long time from ending. “We are seeing some cooling in the Bay Area and the potential for a little moisture of Friday and Saturday,” Black told the Post. “It is important to note that a little bit of precipitation does not end the wildfire threat. A significant warming trend is forecasted toward the middle of next week.” Black noted that the Camp Fire, which decimated the California city of Paradise in 2018, began on November 8 of that year. “Expect significant wildfire potential through the end of November,” Black continued. “Some of California’s deadliest wildfires started in October and even November.” The Piedmont Fire Department encourages all residents to prepare for fire emergencies. He recommends Piedmonters learn how to prevent wildfires by visiting the PFD webpage of the City’s website and www.ReadyForWildfire.org. Images courtesy of Cal Fire Northern California wildfire risk forecast for October and November.
articles.title: Spare the Air alert extended to Thursday as Glass Fire blazes in the North Bay

articles.text: There is an emotional tie to the Piedmont Swimming Pool. We were members for years. Our daughter played high school water polo and was on the Piedmont Swim Team from 2nd grade on. All our children learned to swim there and were so proud to display their white patches. It was an important piece of our lives and the lives of many Piedmonters. This is clearly an emotional issue, as evidenced by the pro-UU letters to the Post. However, as with many other situations we now face, I listen to the experts. I listen to our Chief of Police who stated in April that his “Police Department Facility was not complying with the Essential Services Act”. I listen to our Fire Chief who stated in April that an earthquake would cause “significant structural damage to the Fire Station.” I listen to the financial experts who estimate that the Police and Fire upgrades will cost anywhere from $23 million to $39 million, and who point to the drop in transfer tax revenue year over year. I listen to the financial analysts who wonder how we are going to pay our $7 million sewer system loans, our $13 million Post Employee Benefits Program and our $26 million Net Pension Liability. And I listen to the experienced architects who question the minimal amount of detail in the [Measure UU] plans and the cost estimates for the pool. Would I love to have a new pool? Absolutely. Is this the right time? Absolutely not. I am taking a step back from the emotional side of this issue and relying on the practical side of things. Vote no on UU and let us find a time in the future when we can do this the right way.

Most days I would see someone I knew, and often we would kick for a while together or chat in the locker room. No matter how I felt going to the pool, I always felt great getting out of the water. Every time I swam in that pool, I felt an overwhelming sense of gratitude, hope and possibility. The Piedmont Pool has been a place where people of all ages have formed many happy memories. But pools do not last forever, and Piedmont’s beloved pool is 56 years old and failing. I have watched as the staff has patiently tried to patch it together time and time again, but its age-related deterioration is irreversible. If we want future generations of Piedmonters to have access to a local swimming pool, we need to get going on a replacement. Please join me and our family in supporting Measure UU, so current and future generations can create their own happy memories right here in the middle of our beautiful town. We are voting Yes on Measure UU and hope you do too. –Sarah Pearson, Evan, Emma, Abigail and Nate Seevak Is Council planning another bond next year? By Joe Hurwich Before anyone votes on Measure UU, I think the City Council needs to state its intentions relative to Essential Services upgrades. At the July 6, 2020 City Council Meeting, City Administrator Sara Lillevand discussed “the Budget Advisory & Financial Planning Committee’s recommendation to issue bonds to finance the upgrade of public safety and recreational facilities ….. She indicated since June 29, 2020, Glass Architects has presented a cost estimate for a combined essential services building with an estimated cost of $33-$51 million …. She recommended Council consider placing a standalone, smaller GO bond measure before the voters in November 2020 to replace the Piedmont Community Pool.” So, let me get this straight. 1. The Council knows it needs it will have to ask the voters for $33-$51 million for a new essential services building in the near future. 2. It didn’t have time to form a Community Facilities District (see the same minutes) to facilitate a bond issue prior to the November 2020 election. 3. Therefore, it is trying to sneak in a $20 million bond to finance a new pool knowing full well it will be asking the votes for another, much larger bond issue in the near future to bring essential public services into compliance with California law. 4. Will this ever stop? If you vote in favor of Measure UU, know full well that the City will be asking you to double down and dig deeper into your pockets for much higher priority items very soon. (probably at double the annual property tax cost of the proposed UU bonds.) Why aren’t we considering the most important thing first, one that affects all Piedmonters? Remember that less than ¼ of Piedmonters currently use the pool. The arguments for UU are all general arguments by people that really use the poo. None deal with facts or the real need that Piedmonters have and how to solve it. Nobody suggested spending money necessary to fix the current pool. They just decided that we should throw it away and start over at the expense of all Piedmont families. Everyone knows that Piedmonters will pay for anything, in this case, regardless of who it benefits. I urge you to consider the facts and vote No on Measure UU. For students, life lessons result from teamwork, discipline and friendly competition on the swim teams and water polo teams. The proposed new Aquatic Center for community use will provide even greater space for family gatherings. Please vote yes on UU –Kay and Bob Cheatham Piedmont pool for 21st century means zero-carbon By Tom Webster Last week’s Piedmont Post included a discussion about priorities for when to build new city facilities (a pool, fire and police buildings). To that topic, we would like to add a discussion on how new facilities should be built, in particular a new swimming pool. Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan, approved by City Council in 2018, recommends that municipal facilities and services be zero carbon by 2050. To achieve that objective, the city of Piedmont will have to install solar panels, switch to electric vehicles and stop using natural gas. All new facilities will have to be built for a future of zero carbon emissions. Swimming pools, heated year-round to 70 degrees, require enormous amounts of energy. We examined how to make the proposed pool carbon free. The proposed pool design calls for using green technology to produce 10% of the pool complex electricity from solar panels and 50% of pool heating from solar water heater. That means much of the remaining energy will come from non-renewable sources like natural gas. We explored a scenario that uses a larger on-site solar array to power heat pumps to evaluate designs that could plausibly achieve the zero-carbon standard for the lap pool alone. By directly using solar power collected at the pool and using it to power heat pumps, no natural gas is required to heat the water. The area of the solar array needed to heat a pool with heat pumps depends on the size of the pool and how much of the annual heating load is produced by heat pumps. To heat the pool 100% of the time with solar energy, the solar array would need to be about 70% of the pool size. (see chart from our analysis at the Connect Resources page, https://www.piedmontconnect.org/resources) By using on-site, solar-generated electricity to power heat pumps, and the traditional electricity grid as backup, the heating needs of the lap pool could be met without relying on natural gas. This all-electric pool design would significantly reduce the GHG emissions compared with the proposed design, which uses natural gas. Our analysis shows how different lap pool sizes can be made zero-carbon if sufficient area is available for solar arrays. Our analysis does not account for the energy needs of the fun pool and building, which also must be zero-carbon by 2050. Should Piedmont residents vote in November in favor of building a new pool complex, it behooves the City Council and city staff to ensure that the new facility be built to accommodate a large enough solar array along with heat pumps to eliminate the use of natural gas. By California law, all electricity must be carbon free by 2045, so by building an all-electric lap pool now and relying on the transition to an all-renewable energy grid, the pool complex may be zero-carbon by 2050. It can be viewed at: w w w.pie d mont.ca .gov/se rvices___departments/kcom-tv/ live_content_and_video_archive Spare the Air alert extended to Thursday as Glass Fire blazes in the North Bay By Barry Eitel A “Spare the Air” alert was extended for the San Francisco Bay Area, including Piedmont, through tomorrow, Thursday, October 7, the Bay Area Air Quality Management District said yesterday, Tuesday, October 6. The region’s air quality is being negatively impacted by the destructive Glass Fire that continues to burn through Sonoma and Napa counties. “While most of the Bay Area has experienced cleaner air over the past few days, localized and intermittent smoke impacts will continue near the Glass Fire,”said Jack Broadbent of Bay Air Aire Quality District. “Bay Area residents should continue to be vigilant about air quality conditions over the next couple of days. As fire containment efforts progress and more favorable weather conditions move into the region, we expect more widespread relief from smoke starting this weekend.” When Spare the Air warnings are in effect, people are advised to limit their times outdoors, especially those with who are sensitive to air conditions. Additionally, the use of fireplaces, wood stoves, pellet stoves, outdoor fire pits or other wood-burning devices is prohibited. The Glass Fire began early on September 27. Thousands of people have been evacuated in and aroudn Calistoga, 66,840 acres have burned in the North Bay and 1,411 structures have been destroyed. The fire, which has burned through many vineyards and wineries, is 50 percent contained as of yesterday. The weather in the Bay Area is expected to improve from a wildfire risk standpoint throughout the week, and some precipitation is expected this weekend. However, Fire Chief Bret Black said that wildfire season is a long time from ending. “We are seeing some cooling in the Bay Area and the potential for a little moisture of Friday and Saturday,” Black told the Post. “It is important to note that a little bit of precipitation does not end the wildfire threat. A significant warming trend is forecasted toward the middle of next week.” Black noted that the Camp Fire, which decimated the California city of Paradise in 2018, began on November 8 of that year. “Expect significant wildfire potential through the end of November,” Black continued. “Some of California’s deadliest wildfires started in October and even November.” The Piedmont Fire Department encourages all residents to prepare for fire emergencies. He recommends Piedmonters learn how to prevent wildfires by visiting the PFD webpage of the City’s website and www.ReadyForWildfire.org. articles.text: Local residents Celine McTaggart and her husband, and piedmont resident Rick Arney, founded Californians for Consumer Privacy, the group that spearheaded the campaign for the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) in 2018. It passed unanimously in both the state assembly and senate, which gave Californians the strongest data privacy rights in the United States. This was a huge step forward for consumer privacy in the U.S., but an assault in the legislature the following year (2019) by Big Tech pushed to dilute the rights that would be given to consumers. It was then that a decision to put it on the ballot was made – to allow voters to decide its fate rather than the state legislature. Prop. 24 would allow any pro-privacy amendments with a simple majority of the LegislaNearly one million people signed the petition to put Prop 24 on the ballot. It currently is polling at 81%. Andrew Yang, a presidnetial candidate this year, is Chair of the Prop. 24 Advisory Board, along with Jim Steyer, founder of Common Sense Media. ture, while preventing amendments that hurt consumer privacy. What does Prop. 24 do? 1. Consumers can stop large corporations from using personal data based on race, ethnicity, union membership, sexual orientation, health, etc. 2. It triples fines for abuses of kids’ data, which is more important now since school is online. 3. It creates an enforcement arm to deal with data breaches and abuses of consumer data. The Prop. 24 campaign says, “It is a necessary step to protect California’s leading position in privacy law, to prevent privacy from being gutted in the legislature, and would without a doubt set a strong floor for privacy at the federal level.” For a short history and basis of it qualifying to be on the ballot, see: https://www. caprivacy.org/california-privacy-r ights-act-cpra-qualifies-for-the-november-2020-ballot/ “This is really also about democracy and giving people a choice about their own personal information, like that of their race, ethnicity, and health, and letting them decide who gets to use it – or not.” For more informtion contact Celine Mactaggart at cmactaggart@caprivacy.org. of all that we are facing, to care about surrounding ourselves with quality. The desire to adorn ourPhoto by Mo Saito Photo by Eric Rorer selves and our spaces with art is as old as humankind. People are making art, creating beauty at every moment. Even now. In my industry, we are creating sanctuaries where people can get fortified to go out into the world and help others. That has always been my intent behind being an interior designer (as you may recall from previous columns; also see posts on my blog, tagged Philanthropy, for reference: www.lmbinteriors. com/blog). If we decide we are obligated to feel bad about the plight of others, in a way that depletes us and stops us from taking action, this is simply codependency. What I have seen with my clients is that when they invest time and energy into making their homes support their best selves, they truly do give back. And then use that energy as fuel to keep being, doing, creating, and loving our way to a better world. Laura Martin Bovard is the principal at LMB Interiors, located in downtown Oakland. What does it have to do with the orange sky? This activity, though simple, is a good representation of what happened on September 9th . You can think of the flashlight as representing the sun and its light, traveling all the way to Earth. As it reaches our planet, it must pass through our atmosphere and any other mediums in its path, such as clouds. These natural filters are similar to the cellophane filters we used in the activity. They slow down and change the light as it passes through, changing its wavelength and therefore, the way we see it. When there are thick clouds in the sky it can act like a filter and change the light passing through to appear dark and gray, like what we see on a gloomy day… something we are very familiar with here in the Bay Area.

articles.text: Piedmont firefighters have answered the call to assist in yet another large fire in Northern California as the state trudges through a catastrophic wildfire season. On the morning of September 28, Piedmont Fire Department was requested to the Glass Fire incident for several large spot fires. Engine 2841 left for Calistoga at about 1:30 a.m. The four-man crew assigned to the incident includes Captain Mike Carlisle, Engineer Alan Grace, Firefighter Sandor Lengyel, and Firefighter/Paramedic Brian Gidney. The firefighters went to work immediately in Calistoga, rescuing residents and performing structure protection where possible. Piedmont responded along with Fremont and Berkeley Fire Departments. “The crew is expected to be assigned to the Glass Fire for at least a few more days,” Fire Chief Bret Black confirmed. As of October 5 the Glass Fire had burned over 65,000 acres and was located near North Fork Crystal Springs Road in St. Helena. It has impacted Napa and Sonoma counties. Through Sunday night, the fire burned actively due to low humidity and high temperatures. Aggressive mop-up work continued in areas where the fire’s forward progress had stopped, according to Cal Fire. Crews were working aggressively on Monday to construct and reinforce existing control lines. As of Monday afternoon, 1,235 residential and commercial structures had been destroyed, including much of the famed Meadowood resort. A total of 27 crews have been assigned to assist in containing the fire. This year has marked a record fire season for the state, with a total of four million acres burned by October 2020. While many of California’s largest fires occur in late summer, the deadliest and most destructive blazes tend to occur at the end of the dry season, from September to December. Cal Fire noted that, while wildfires are a natural part of California’s landscape, the fire season in California and across the West is starting earlier and ending later each year. “Climate change is considered a key driver of this trend. Warmer spring and summer temperatures, reduced snowpack, and earlier spring snowmelt create longer and more intense dry seasons that increase moisture stress on vegetation and make forests more susceptible to severe wildfire,” Cal Fire stated. The length of California’s fire season is estimated to have increased by 75 days across the Sierras and seems to correspond with an increase in the extent of forest fires across the state. upgrades, or play structure improvements. “We work closely with Carol Cramer, the school principal, and try to support her with anything she needs,” said Learn. “Our main effort is trying to bring back a little bit of normal life so we can kind of forget about the rest of the chaos swirling around,” said Learn with a grin. articles.text: According to the Alameda County Registrar of Voter, to avoid large gatherings of people only one voting location will be open in Piedmont on election day, November 3. The Veterans’ Memorial Building at 401 Highland Avenue will serve as the city’s voting location for in-person voting this election, but it will be open three days instead of only on election day. Residents can vote at the Veterans’ Memorial Building on Saturday, October 31, and on Monday and Tuesday, November 2 - 3, from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Any resident of Alameda County can come to the Veterans Hall and cast their ballot, or drop off their absentee ballot. They may also put their absentee ballot in the secure ballot box located on Highland Way near the two mailboxes. Ballots may be dropped off anytime up to 8 p.m. on November 4. A list of all polling locations in Alameda County is available online at https:// w w w.acgov.org /rov_ app/ pollinglist. The Registrar of Voters was scheduled to began mailing ballots to all voters this week, starting on Monday, October 5. Residents who have not received a sample ballot may contact the registrar’s office at (510) 272-6933. The local election will include names of candidates for two seats on the Piedmont City Council and three seats on the School Board. Other noteworthy elections include the President of the United States, United States Representative, and Assemblymember, as well as several statewide measures, special district measures, and two City of Piedmont measures: Measure TT and Measure UU.
